Historically Black Protestant.beliefs: God created all things and acts in history to deliver the oppressed, as in the Exodus; humanity is fallen and is saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection bring forgiveness and new life. Believers hope for eternal life with God and expect God's justice both in the world to come and in this one. Authority rests on the Bible as God's word, preached and heard in community, with the Holy Spirit's guidance stressed especially in Holiness and Pentecostal churches.
Historically Black Protestant.values: Personal faith and daily prayer; the church as extended family and center of community life; preaching, gospel music and expressive, participatory worship; hope and endurance through suffering; the God-given dignity and equality of every person; education, mutual aid, service and civic duty, including voting.
Historically Black Protestant.forbids: Sexual immorality, drunkenness and drug misuse, profanity, gambling and occult practice are widely taught against; Holiness churches such as COGIC also ask for modest dress and limits on worldly entertainment. Racism is treated as a sin against God, not only a social wrong: most Black adults say opposing racism is essential to their faith (Pew 2021).
Historically Black Protestant.family: The large bodies officially teach that marriage is between a man and a woman (AME Discipline, reaffirmed 2024; COGIC; NBC USA 2012 statement); the Progressive National Baptist Convention leaves same-sex blessings to each congregation, and members' views vary (56% favored same-sex marriage in Pew's 2023-24 study). Women are ordained in the AME, AME Zion, CME and PNBC; COGIC does not ordain women as pastors but has a large Women's Department and honored church mothers; National Baptist congregations decide for themselves. Elders and the church family share in raising children. Identity is marked by baptism, Sunday worship, choir and youth ministries, revivals and church anniversaries.
Historically Black Protestant.stories: Stories are judged by whether they honor God, tell the truth about suffering and hope, and treat people with dignity. Bible stories of deliverance (Moses, Joseph, Daniel) are the model: the faithful endure, God makes a way, and the lowly are lifted up. Fantasy is accepted by many families; Holiness and Pentecostal families are more wary of spells, spirits and the occult, which they may see as spiritually real. How Black characters are drawn and portrayed is often noticed.
Historically Black Protestant.range: Seven large denominations studied by Lincoln and Mamiya (National Baptist Convention USA, National Baptist Convention of America, Progressive National Baptist Convention, AME, AME Zion, CME, Church of God in Christ), plus Black Missionary and independent Baptist, Holiness, Pentecostal and nondenominational churches. Baptist congregations are self-governing; COGIC and Holiness churches keep stricter standards; the PNBC is the most socially activist and on some questions the most open.

topics.Alcohol: Abstinence widely taught in Black Methodist, Baptist and Holiness churches; COGIC forbids alcohol. Drinking shown as fun or grown-up is a common concern.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Drug misuse condemned; many churches run recovery ministries; tobacco discouraged.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Witchcraft, fortune-telling and conjure rejected (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); spiritual warfare taken seriously in Pentecostal and Holiness churches. Fantasy magic is debated, and many families are cautious with spells, summoning and spirits.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Exclusive claims of Christ (John 14:6) held alongside respect for neighbors of other faiths; other gods shown as real and good can be a concern.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Nonviolent resistance of the Civil Rights movement honored; revenge rejected (Romans 12:19); protecting the vulnerable valued; concern about glorified street and gang violence.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Purity and modesty taught; sexual content and fan service a concern.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Official teaching in most bodies holds marriage to be a man and a woman; the PNBC leaves it to local churches and members are divided, so same-sex romance is a concern for many families but not all.
topics.Gender roles and family: Strong women's leadership in church life; women ordained in AME, AME Zion, CME and PNBC, not as pastors in COGIC; practice varies among National Baptists.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Profanity and taking God's name in vain a concern (Exodus 20:7); racial slurs a serious concern.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Honor parents and elders (Ephesians 6:1-3); respect for rightful authority, joined to a prophetic tradition that confronts unjust laws and rulers (Exodus; Amos 5:24).
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Death faced with hope of resurrection and going home to God; funerals (homegoing services) are major community events; suicide met with grief, prayer and growing attention to mental health.
topics.Lying and deception: Lying sinful (Proverbs 12:22); deceptive heroes worth discussing.

Historically Black Protestant.media: No denomination-wide media code. Philippians 4:8 is a common test, and Holiness churches teach separation from worldly entertainment. Many families also ask how Black people are shown, valuing dignity and fair representation alongside clean content.
Historically Black Protestant.grading_note: Grade as a Bible-centered tradition whose personal morality is close to the Baptist and Pentecostal frames but whose reading of the Bible puts deliverance and justice at the center. Tends to welcome: deliverance from bondage or oppression, faith and prayer that carry people through suffering, hope that does not give up, loyalty to family and community, elders' wisdom, standing up to injustice (especially without hatred), protecting the weak, redemption and second chances, education and self-improvement. Tends to worry about: occult or demonic power shown as good, sexual content and fan service, profanity and mockery of God or the church, revenge celebrated, despair with no hope, and racial caricature (a depiction concern; it lowers the grade only when the story's message endorses contempt for a people). Same-sex romance is a concern for many families but not all; note it rather than treating it as decisive. Stories that join justice themes with personal holiness grade highest.

Atheist.beliefs: Atheists lack belief in any god (American Atheists' definition); most see the natural world as all there is and expect no afterlife, though there is no shared creed, scripture or leader. Pew (2023) found 78% of atheists say science can in principle explain everything, while about one in five still believe in some higher power or spiritual force, not the God of the Bible. Authority rests on evidence and reason, with each person reaching their own conclusions.
Atheist.values: Honesty about what can and cannot be known; reason and evidence; not hurting people and logic as the main moral guides (86% and 87% call them very important, Pew 2023); freedom of conscience; separation of church and state; science education; meaning found in relationships, work and this life.
Atheist.forbids: No formal prohibitions. Common concerns are religious pressure on children, claims presented as true without evidence, and harm or cruelty.
Atheist.family: No set family pattern; equal roles and same-sex marriage are widely accepted (88% of the religiously unaffiliated favor same-sex marriage, Pew 2023-24). Parents usually explain the reasons behind rules, want children to think for themselves and learn about many religions, and leave final beliefs to the child (Dale McGowan; Christel Manning). Identity is marked lightly: some join local atheist or freethought groups, Secular Student Alliance chapters, or advocacy groups such as American Atheists and the Freedom From Religion Foundation (Madison, Wisconsin).
Atheist.stories: Myths, gods, demons and magic are welcomed as fiction and cultural heritage, and religious stories are often enjoyed as literature. Concern arises when a story teaches that faith is needed to be good, that doubters are wicked, or that unbelief is punished.
Atheist.range: From quiet, private nonbelievers to active members of atheist and church-state groups; from those who see religion as mostly harmful (73% of atheists say it does more harm than good, Pew 2023) to those who value it as culture. Mostly but not entirely left-leaning (78% Democratic or lean). Distinct from the Secular humanist frame (an organized positive philosophy) and the Secular progressive frame (a political-values frame): the only shared trait is not believing in gods.

topics.Alcohol: Responsible adult use; concern for minors.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Evidence-based concern about harm and addiction.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Not a concern as fiction; concern when real-world supernatural claims (fortune-telling, faith healing) are presented as true.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Fine as story material; concern when one faith is shown as the true answer or nonbelievers are cast as villains.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Judged by harm; concern about glorified cruelty; violence done in a god's name especially noticed.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Not framed as sin; concern about exploitation, consent and sexualizing minors.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Profanity a mild concern; blasphemy not a concern.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Questioning authority, including religious authority, valued; parents explain reasons rather than demand obedience.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Death is the end of the person; afterlives in stories are fiction; meaning comes from how one lives; suicide approached through mental-health care.
topics.Lying and deception: Honesty, including intellectual honesty, highly valued.

Atheist.media: No media rules. Families tend to favor curiosity, science and free expression and to oppose censorship; they notice stories that present belief as the only road to goodness or treat doubters as villains.
Atheist.grading_note: Grade the story's conclusions about belief, not its fantasy furniture: gods, spirits and magic inside a fictional world do not lower the grade. Tends to welcome: characters who question, investigate and test claims; goodness that comes from empathy rather than command; meaning built in this life; heroes who solve problems by their own effort and reason; exposure of manipulative religious or cult authority; respect for free thought. Tends to worry about: stories whose resolution is that faith or prayer is the real answer, conversion arcs that treat unbelief as a flaw to be cured, skeptics punished or mocked as fools, and real-world supernatural claims presented as fact. A story set in a world with real gods can still grade well if its characters act from human compassion and choice.

Agnostic.beliefs: Agnostics hold that whether God exists is unknown or cannot be known; T. H. Huxley coined the word in 1869 and called it a method rather than a creed. Many stay open: Pew (2023) found 67% of agnostics believe in God or some higher power and 61% believe there is something spiritual beyond the natural world, though they name no religion. Authority rests on reason and evidence, with honest admission of the limits of knowledge.
Agnostic.values: Intellectual humility and open-mindedness; reason and evidence; tolerance of differing beliefs; not hurting people and logic as moral guides (88% each call them very important, Pew 2023); freedom to keep exploring.
Agnostic.forbids: No formal prohibitions. Common concerns are dogmatism and certainty claimed without evidence, from religious or anti-religious voices alike; pressure on children to adopt a belief; and harm or cruelty.
Agnostic.family: No set pattern; equal roles and same-sex marriage are widely accepted. Parents often expose children to several traditions and leave the choice to them; some attend a congregation for community or for a spouse's faith (Christel Manning). Identity is mostly private, and holidays are often kept as family and cultural occasions.
Agnostic.stories: Gods, spirits and mysteries are welcomed as ways of wondering about big questions, and endings that leave a mystery open are often appreciated. Concern arises when a story insists on certainty either way: that one faith is the only truth, or that all belief is foolish.
Agnostic.range: From near-atheists who simply will not claim certainty to seekers who believe in a higher power but no religion (41% describe themselves as spiritual, Pew 2023). About half (51%) say religion does more harm than good, while 38% say it does equal good and harm. Nearly half are college graduates (48%), and most lean left (71% Democratic or lean). Distinct from Atheist (lack of belief) and from the Secular humanist and Secular progressive values frames: the defining trait is not knowing.

topics.Alcohol: Responsible adult use; concern for minors.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Evidence-based concern about harm and addiction.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Not a concern as fiction; mystery and the unexplained are welcomed.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Respectful, curious portrayals welcomed; concern when one faith is shown as the only truth or when believers are mocked.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Concern about glorified violence; fanaticism of any kind noticed.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Concern about exploitation, consent and sexualizing minors.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Mild concern; blasphemy not a concern, though gratuitous mockery of believers may be.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Questioning valued; skepticism toward anyone claiming final answers.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: An open question; stories that imagine an afterlife are welcomed as wonder; suicide approached through mental-health care.
topics.Lying and deception: Honesty valued, including honesty about what one does not know.

Agnostic.media: No rules. Families tend to value stories that raise big questions honestly, present more than one view fairly and leave room for the reader to decide.
Agnostic.grading_note: Grade for openness and honesty about the big questions. Tends to welcome: characters who wrestle with doubt without being punished for it, fair portrayal of several worldviews, humility, wonder at mystery, ethics grounded in empathy, open endings about what lies beyond. Tends to worry about: preachy certainty in either direction, conversion or deconversion as the only acceptable ending, contempt for believers or for doubters, and charismatic leaders who demand unquestioning faith shown as admirable. Gods and spirits as fiction do not lower the grade; a story that answers every spiritual question with a firm doctrine may grade lower than for Atheist or Nothing in particular, and a story that sneers at all belief may grade lower than for Atheist.

Nothing in particular.beliefs: Not a belief system: people who do not identify with any religion, nor as atheist or agnostic. Most still believe in God or a higher power (83%, Pew 2023); many believe in a soul (78%), heaven (50%) and hell (41%), and 19% pray daily, though few attend services. Authority is personal: what makes sense to them, how they were raised, and a sense that what goes around comes around (54% call it very important in moral choices).
Nothing in particular.values: Not hurting people (80% very important) and logic and reason (79%); family, friends and loyalty; fairness; staying out of trouble; personal freedom. Many value spirituality without religion: 60% describe themselves as spiritual or say spirituality is very important to them (Pew 2023).
Nothing in particular.forbids: No formal prohibitions. Many dislike religious institutions or religious pressure; concerns center on harm, cruelty and content beyond a child's age.
Nothing in particular.family: Family forms vary; most accept same-sex marriage (the unaffiliated as a whole favor it 88%, Pew 2023-24). Most parents want children to choose for themselves. Some are believers without a church who pray or read the Bible at home; others are spiritual seekers who mix traditions, and others are simply indifferent (Christel Manning's four types). Identity is marked by family traditions, with religious holidays often kept as family occasions.
Nothing in particular.stories: Gods, spirits, fate and an afterlife are welcomed and often taken half-seriously; many readers like the sense that the universe is fair or that loved ones watch over us. Religious content is fine when it is not preachy; concern arises with stories that push a religion, or that attack belief.
Nothing in particular.range: The largest unaffiliated group (19% of U.S. adults; 63% of nones): from people who believe in God but skip church, through spiritual-but-not-religious seekers, to those who rarely think about religion. On average less formally educated (27% college graduates) and more politically mixed (54% Democratic or lean) than atheists and agnostics, and less involved in civic groups; scholars such as Ryan Burge note many are less connected to institutions of all kinds, not only religious ones. Not the same as the Secular humanist or Secular progressive frames: many hold spiritual beliefs and few belong to secular organizations.

topics.Alcohol: Responsible adult use; concern for minors.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Not usually a concern; many believe spirits or spiritual energy may be real, so ghosts and spirits can feel meaningful rather than purely fictional.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Generally open; concern about any religion shown as pushy, or about mockery of belief.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Concern about glorified violence; fairness and payback themes resonate.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Mostly accepting, with more variety than among atheists and agnostics.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Distrust of institutions is common; family authority respected.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Many believe in heaven or some afterlife, and loved ones watching over us is a common comfort; suicide approached through mental-health care.
topics.Lying and deception: Honesty and loyalty to friends valued.

Nothing in particular.media: No rules; families decide case by case, mostly by age-appropriateness, kindness, and whether a story is enjoyable rather than preachy.
Nothing in particular.grading_note: Do not grade this frame as a copy of Secular humanist: most of these families believe in God or a higher power, many in an afterlife and in spirits. Tends to welcome: loyalty to family and friends, everyday decency, fairness and karma-like justice, a personal spiritual sense that does not demand membership, reunion with or protection by the dead, hope, and finding your own path. Tends to worry about: preachy religion or preachy anti-religion, despair and nihilism, cruelty celebrated, and institutions (religious or not) that control people. Spiritual-but-open stories (gods, souls, fate) usually grade higher here than for Atheist; stories that end in a call to one exclusive faith grade somewhat lower than for the Christian frames but are not rejected.

Hindu ideas.label: Hindu ideas
row: Hindu ideas

Life is ordered by dharma (right order and one's duty) and by karma, the soul passes through many births (samsara), and liberation (moksha) comes through right action, knowledge, or loving devotion (bhakti) to God, who can enter the world in forms called avatars.
Gods and demons drawn from Indian myth, reincarnated heroes and avatars, characters bound by caste or duty, or a hero told to do their duty without clinging to the result.

Buddhist ideas.label: Buddhist ideas
row: Buddhist ideas

Life as usually lived is marked by suffering (dukkha) that comes from craving, everything is impermanent and there is no lasting self, and a path of ethics, meditation and wisdom (or, in Pure Land teaching, trust in Amida Buddha's vow) leads out of rebirth to nirvana, with compassion for all beings at its heart.

Monks and temples, karma following a character across lives, peace found by letting go of a grudge or attachment, mercy toward enemies, and in Japanese works, funerals, family altars, Obon visits from the dead, Zen training, and Buddhist hells judged by King Enma.

Bushido / honor code.label: Bushido / honor code
row: Bushido / honor code
A warrior should live by a code of honor: loyalty to one's lord or cause above self, rectitude, courage, self-control and courtesy, and readiness to die rather than live in disgrace.
A swordsman who keeps his word at any cost, loyalty to a master or clan, duels fought by the rules, shame worse than death, ritual suicide, and stories asking whether the code is noble or a trap.

Patriotism / nationalism.label: Patriotism / nationalism
row: Patriotism / nationalism

Love of and loyalty to one's country and people, with a readiness to serve and sacrifice for it; in its fuller political form, nationalism, the belief that the nation is the main unit of political life, should govern itself, and has first claim on its members' loyalty.

Heroes defending a homeland, soldiers serving their country, the founding or unification of a nation, rival peoples at war, and stories asking whether love of country is noble or has turned into hatred of others.

Pacifism / nonviolence.label: Pacifism / nonviolence
row: Pacifism / nonviolence

Violence, and above all war, is wrong and should be refused on principle, even at cost to oneself, and conflicts should be met by nonviolent means such as forgiveness, persuasion, protest, or bearing wrong rather than doing it.
A hero who vows never to kill, a warrior who lays down the sword, characters who break a cycle of revenge, or a story showing the horror of war and calling for peace.

Duty ethics (deontology).label: Duty ethics
row: Duty ethics

Some acts are right or wrong in themselves, whatever their results: we must keep promises, tell the truth, and treat every person as an end and never merely as a tool, even when breaking the rule would bring a better outcome.
A character who will not lie or break a promise even to win, who refuses to sacrifice one innocent to save many, or who defends the law against a vigilante's results.

Liberalism.label: Liberalism (rights and consent)
row: Liberalism (rights and consent)

Each person has equal rights and freedoms that government exists to protect, power is legitimate only with the consent of the governed and under the rule of law, and people of differing beliefs should tolerate one another.
Constitutions and elections defended against a tyrant, fair trials and rights for the accused, free speech and religious tolerance, and heroes who fight for a free republic rather than a good king.

Anarchism.label: Anarchism
row: Anarchism
No state or ruler has a rightful claim to govern others by force, and society should run instead on free agreement, mutual aid and local cooperation without coercive hierarchy.
Rebels and outlaws who want no rulers at all, not just better ones, free towns or crews without a chain of command, and stories showing a stateless society as freedom or as chaos.

frames_add.concerns: Psychic powers shown as partly real, a staged resurrection parodying sacred things, and drinking, gambling and a mafia setting (v9-15).

frames_add.aligns: Staged miracles are exposed as frauds and science (Kiriko's vaccine) ends the plague, while critical thinking about every messiah is the lesson.
frames_add.concerns: Psychic powers are left partly real, and the heroes themselves risk becoming objects of devotion.

frames_add.aligns: A charismatic leader demanding blind faith is condemned, yet a Catholic church and priest are shown sympathetically, so belief itself is not sneered at.
frames_add.concerns: Dread and mass death, and the story's suspicion of every savior may feel one-sided to some readers.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to childhood friends, everyday decency and owning up to a past wrong win against a controlling institution.
frames_add.concerns: A long, fearful story of cults, pandemics and murder that may be heavy for younger teens.

frames_add.aligns: A false messiah is unmasked as a wounded man, hidden sin comes to light (Numbers 32:23) and Kenji confesses and apologizes to the boy he wronged (ch. 15; 1 John 1:9).
frames_add.concerns: A violent opening death (ch. 1), Kanna's psychic powers left standing, and a secular tone with no prayer or church.

frames_add.aligns: Fairness, owning up to what you did and not letting a lonely child become invisible are at the heart of it, and the old friends reunite (v2).

frames_add.concerns: Child marriage and harsh customs shown with little critique; nudity involving a 12-year-old.

frames_add.aligns: Family, loyalty, hospitality and good humor; those who use custom for greed or control lose.
frames_add.concerns: The 12-year-old husband and the undressing scene; customs that limit women's choices.

frames_add.aligns: Every person's God-given dignity shows in its warm portrait of Deaf life, Itsuomi learns another's language out of love and serves poor children abroad (Sign 31, 43), and the couple marry with the father's blessing (Sign 56-61).
frames_add.concerns: Cohabitation and an implied first night before marriage (v9-v13; Hebrews 13:4) and a bar with regular drinking as a main setting.

frames_add.aligns: Human worth and capability, empathy built through effort, and problems solved by honest talk and practical tools (Sign 30, 37), with no religious frame.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond drinking and the gentle adult intimacy (v9-v13).

frames_add.aligns: Two people from different worlds reach each other by listening; the story respects difference without preaching (Signs 1, 56).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; adult intimacy is implied rather than shown (v13).

frames_add.aligns: Kindness, loyalty, family blessing and a couple who choose each other for life; friends rally around those who lose out (Sign 47).
frames_add.concerns: Rated 16+ by its publisher for cohabitation, implied intimacy and bar drinking.

frames_add.aligns: A bully confesses, makes restitution like Zacchaeus (Luke 19:8) and learns sign language; a disabled girl's dignity is upheld, two mothers sacrifice for their children, and both suicidal characters come to see their lives as worth living (ch. 43-62).
frames_add.concerns: A suicide plan and a suicide attempt (v1-2, ch. 42-43), detailed bullying of a deaf child (v1), coarse language, and healing that never names God.

frames_add.aligns: Worth, repair and meaning come from empathy and human relationships, with no religious framing needed.
frames_add.concerns: Neither suicidal character is shown getting professional help (to verify).

frames_add.aligns: An honest, many-sided look at guilt and forgiveness that leaves room for readers of any faith or none to draw their own conclusions.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the suicide content.

frames_add.aligns: Everyday decency, owning up to harm, second chances and friends who show up when it matters.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide themes and bullying make it 13+ (Common Sense Media) or 14+ (Raising Children Network) for the film.

frames_add.aligns: A hunted minority treated as less than human is shown as wronged, the state's torture labs (v2) and Sato's terror in the name of liberation (ch. 19) are both condemned, and loyal friends (Kaito, Nakano) risk their lives for others.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic torture, vivisection and dismemberment throughout, characters routinely killing themselves to 'reset' (v9, v12, v16-17), and a hero who long reasons that some lives count more than others (ch. 43).

frames_add.aligns: Human dignity is defended without religion, reason and empathy defeat both the torturing state and the terrorist, and Kei still aims to become a doctor (epilogue).
frames_add.concerns: Heavy gore, the casual self-killing 'reset,' and a cynical view of crowds and government.

frames_add.aligns: Hard questions about what a self is (decapitation creates a new mind) and whether lives can be weighed are raised honestly and left for the reader, with no religious or anti-religious preaching.
frames_add.concerns: Torture and gore far beyond most teen fiction, and a charismatic mass murderer whom many fans admire.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, fairness for those treated as lab animals, and the fall of both a controlling state program and a cruel terrorist.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic torture and terror attacks, routine self-killing as a game mechanic, and a bleak picture of how fear turns neighbors into bounty hunters.

frames_add.aligns: Tyranny and the abuse of poor villages are clearly condemned, and the oppressed are delivered from a corrupt court (ch. 78).
frames_add.concerns: Justice comes by assassination and revenge (Romans 12:19), the winners torture Honest and execute a child Emperor (ch. 78); sexual violence recurs, including against children (ch. 23.5, 45-46), with fan service and strong profanity.

frames_add.aligns: The one religious movement is exposed as a front for manipulation (vols. 6-9), and the heroes refuse to dress up killing as justice.
frames_add.concerns: Torture of prisoners by the winners and little due process (ch. 78); sexual violence, including against children, used as villain shorthand.

frames_add.aligns: The story does not claim certainty that its revolution is right and leaves the new nation's future open.
frames_add.concerns: Extreme gore, recurring sexual violence including against children, and executions with little mercy.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal found family, protecting the weak, and a corrupt elite brought down.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty and despair dominate, nearly every hero dies, and sexual violence including against children recurs (ch. 23.5, 45-46).

frames_add.aligns: Tyranny and state experiments on children end in ruin, a drugged cult that worships a child is exposed as false (v4), and drug dependence is shown as bondage.
frames_add.concerns: Spirit mediumship and psychic power are shown as good and decisive; extreme violence, teen drug use, and sexual captivity and an attempted rape involving teen characters (v4-5); the hero's early treatment of women is never judged.

frames_add.aligns: A cult that worships a drugged child-emperor is exposed as manipulation, and ordinary survivors rebuild without any god.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual exploitation involving teen characters shown without a clear moral voice; teen drug use; the ending turns to cosmic transcendence.

frames_add.aligns: A sincere temple and a manipulative cult are both shown, and the ending leaves what lies 'beyond this world' an open mystery (v6).
frames_add.concerns: Extreme violence, drugs, and sexual exploitation involving teen characters.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends survive what no institution could control and build a community of their own.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty and destruction on a vast scale, teen drug use, and sexual exploitation involving teen characters (v1-2, v4-5).

frames_add.aligns: Friends lay down their lives (John 15:13), predation and the Beach's cruelty are condemned, and the story chooses life over despair.
frames_add.concerns: Two attempted sexual assaults on a high-school girl (ch. 20, 39) and sexual content involving high-school characters (ch. 10, 44); suicide and self-harm; hope rests on people alone.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is made by people with no god required; reason, cooperation and a plural set of human answers to why we live (Final Chapter).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content and assault involving high-school characters; cruelty shown for shock.

frames_add.aligns: The Joker is neither God nor Devil (ch. 63) and a scientist allows that some things cannot be explained (ch. 64); the afterlife is left open.
frames_add.concerns: The same content involving high-school characters; heavy violence.

frames_add.aligns: Friends' sacrifice and love carry Arisu back to life; the in-between world hints that death is not simply the end.
frames_add.concerns: Extreme violence, suicide content and the attempted assaults.

frames_add.aligns: Perseverance through repeated suffering, protecting others, and sacrificial love (John 15:13), with war shown as costly rather than glorious.
frames_add.concerns: A gun-in-mouth suicide test is played as black comedy (likely ch. 2-3); graphic battle gore; a crude nickname; a killing presented as the only way out (likely ch. 16-17).

frames_add.aligns: Keiji grows by trial, error and reason with no supernatural help, and the author's point is that one life matters because when you die it is over.
frames_add.concerns: The suicide test is played for laughs and needs a safe-messaging talk; the ending's 'only way' logic is disputed by critics.

frames_add.aligns: The story asks hard questions about sacrifice and fate without offering a doctrine, and leaves Keiji to carry his grief honestly.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic violence, the suicide gag, and an ending that settles a moral dilemma by killing.

frames_add.aligns: Comradeship, perseverance and a love that gives everything for others.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic deaths, the suicide test played as a joke, and a hero who ends alone and feared.

frames_add.aligns: Honesty wins over pretending, a girl stands up for a bullied classmate (v1), a grieving son reconciles with his brother and father (likely v4; Ephesians 6:1-4), and a teacher keeps a proper boundary with a student.
frames_add.concerns: Teen dating is not aimed at marriage, Kou's forceful kiss (ch. 21) and pin-down scene (likely v3) are treated as romance, and grief is healed with no word of faith or hope beyond this life.

frames_add.aligns: Grief is faced honestly in this life and healed through human connection, with no supernatural framing.
frames_add.concerns: Consent in Kou's forceful kiss and pin-down is not examined.

frames_add.aligns: Characters admit doubt, fear and guilt and are not punished for it, and the story preaches nothing about the big questions.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the forceful kiss (ch. 21).

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friendship, family repair, being true to yourself and a hopeful ending at the shrine where the story began (v13).
frames_add.concerns: Kou's cold and sometimes rough treatment of Futaba.

frames_add.aligns: Students the school wrote off are given dignity and an education, abusers are defeated, and a former killer is changed by one woman's kindness (ch. 134-140), a picture of redemption and a second chance.
frames_add.concerns: Children train to kill their teacher as the premise, he chooses to die at their hands (ch. 177), and an adult teacher's kissing of students and the 'Bitch-sensei' nickname are played as jokes (from ch. 8-12).

frames_add.aligns: Education, reason, effort and human relationships transform the students, with no supernatural answers, and the government's cold logic is questioned.
frames_add.concerns: Comic kissing of students by an adult teacher (from ch. 8-12) and porn gags; the willing death needs a careful talk.

frames_add.aligns: The class argues both sides of killing one to save many (ch. 143-146), and even the harsh principal is given a sympathetic reason (likely ch. 121-124).
frames_add.concerns: The adult-on-student comedy and dated gender gags, such as Nagisa's forced cross-dressing (ch. 66).

frames_add.aligns: A teacher who believes in every kid, loyal classmates and a legacy that lives on in his students (ch. 178-180) reward everyday decency.
frames_add.concerns: A bullied student's suicide in a backstory, an emotionally abusive mother (ch. 112), and the premise of students trying to kill a teacher.

frames_add.aligns: Persecution of a people by descent (armbands and internment, ch. 86-88) is condemned, revenge is shown to spread hatred, and forgiveness is honored (the Blouse family toward Gabi), in line with Romans 12:17-21.
frames_add.concerns: The Titans' power comes from a pact with a being called a devil (ch. 122), there is no hope beyond death, the hero becomes a mass killer (ch. 123-131), and a suicide attempt is shown (ch. 95).

frames_add.aligns: A wall cult and a lying monarchy hide the truth (vols. 9-17) while truth-seeking by Armin and Hange is honored, and meaning is found in this life's small moments (ch. 137 area).
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: genocide, child soldiers and a suicide attempt (ch. 95) need mature readers.

frames_add.aligns: Each side gets a fair hearing, Ymir's origin and the Paths stay mysterious, and the ending leaves the reader to weigh Eren rather than handing down a verdict.
frames_add.concerns: Readers disagree sharply on what it endorses, so younger readers may need help with the nationalism and genocide themes.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, fairness to the enemy once you know them, and the dead honored by those who carry on (Erwin, Hange) run through the story.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic violence, the death of most of humanity in the Rumbling and an ending where war returns can feel hopeless.

frames_add.aligns: Hard work, education and perseverance are rewarded, a long chaste promise ends in a proposal, and cheating fails (Colossians 3:23).
frames_add.concerns: Women are often treated dismissively (vol. 1 lines; criticized by several reviewers); overwork that costs health; adult drinking; talk of fan service.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning comes from human creativity, partnership and honest effort, with no supernatural claims.
frames_add.concerns: Several reviewers call the treatment of women sexist; overwork is often praised.

frames_add.aligns: A grounded story about chasing a dream that makes no claims about the big questions.
frames_add.concerns: Career and rankings as the measure of a life; narrow gender roles.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to a partner, fair play among rivals and a promise kept over years; rivals help each other.
frames_add.concerns: The uncle's death from overwork and Mashiro's hospital stay as the cost of ambition; dismissive lines about girls.

frames_add.aligns: A teen who was owned and trafficked fights his way free; the powerful men who bought children are exposed (ch. 17-18); loyalty and self-sacrifice.
frames_add.concerns: Recounted and implied sexual abuse of a child and teen (ch. 10, vol. 2); constant killing and revenge; strong language; little hope beyond human love; homoerotic framing that families may weigh.

frames_add.aligns: Human bonds as the source of meaning; cruelty and drugs used as weapons are condemned; no supernatural frame.
frames_add.concerns: Exploitation on the page; vigilante killing; critics say gay men appear only as predators.

frames_add.aligns: No easy answers about guilt, violence or freedom; the cost of every choice is shown.
frames_add.concerns: The abuse content and the near-constant violence.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, friendship and a love that asks nothing (Eiji); abusers lose everything.
frames_add.concerns: Child sexual abuse is central (though off-page) and the hero dies; a hard read for younger teens.

frames_add.aligns: Deliverance of the poor below from an elite above that exploits them; protecting the helpless; self-sacrifice and rebirth at the end (Epilogue).
frames_add.concerns: Constant gore and some nudity; a heroine who revels in killing; a demon-named villain (Zapan); no God in the story's world, and the heaven above is false.

frames_add.aligns: What makes a person human is answered without the supernatural; the false heaven of Zalem is exposed (Battle 48); science shown with ethical limits.
frames_add.concerns: Heavy gore; the bleak middle volumes.

frames_add.aligns: Big questions about mind, body and self left open; the Tree of Life ending keeps a sense of mystery.
frames_add.concerns: Gore and body horror; long stretches of grief.

frames_add.aligns: Protecting the weak, loyalty, and reunion with a loved one at the end; the rich who exploit others are exposed.
frames_add.concerns: Gore and despair; Kodansha rates it 16+.

frames_add.aligns: Segregation, profiling and laws keeping groups apart are shown as wrong (ch. 99, 193), self-control is the hero's path (Galatians 5:23), and mercy is shown even to a killer.
frames_add.concerns: Teen sexual activity is shown without judgment (Haru), hunger and sexual desire are fused, no God exists in the story's world, and a parent's suicide and a suicide attempt appear.

frames_add.aligns: Characters choose their values against their biology by reason, effort and friendship, with no higher power to rescue them.
frames_add.concerns: The predation-as-desire metaphor raises consent questions (ch. 3, 25), and the suicide material (Leano, Melon) needs care.

frames_add.aligns: The story wrestles honestly with whether nature decides who we are and leaves room for doubt, with no doctrine pushed.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content between teens, gore in the black-market arcs, and a parent's presumed suicide.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friendship across group lines, everyday decency, and a dead mother's spirit appearing to her son.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content between teens, frequent violence, and despair in Melon's story.

frames_add.aligns: Hard work, loyalty and courage against bullies (v3-4) and against a mogul who blacklists the band (v18-24), with a gift developed through practice and a brotherhood that will not let its members quit.
frames_add.concerns: Peeping and underwear-theft gags (likely v1), an adult mentor's lechery played for laughs, a skinny-dipping scene with 14-year-olds (v2-3), drinking, profanity and gun violence; a song called Devil's Way (v29-32).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is made through skill, art and friendship, and success comes from practice and persistence rather than luck or providence.
frames_add.concerns: Peeping played as comedy (likely v1) and the scene with 14-year-olds (v2-3).

frames_add.aligns: No doctrine is pressed; a boy who thinks he is nobody finds his own path and voice.
frames_add.concerns: Consent questions in the peeping and lechery gags, and the skinny-dipping scene with 14-year-olds (v2-3).

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty among friends, a kind if crude mentor, and controlling industry bosses and gangsters beaten by the band's music (v32).
frames_add.concerns: Crude sexual humor in the early volumes (v1-4), drinking and gangster gun violence.

frames_add.aligns: Guts endures crushing suffering and slowly turns from revenge to protecting Casca and refugees (v35-41), in line with Romans 12:19 and care for the lowly, and religious cruelty by the powerful is condemned.
frames_add.concerns: Witchcraft is shown as wise and healing (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), the church appears mainly as a torturer (v16-21), and explicit sexual violence, including against a child (v3-4, v13), weighs very heavily.

frames_add.aligns: Evil is born from human minds rather than a devil, fanaticism and the inquisition are exposed (Mozgus, v16-21), and meaning comes from human will and care for companions.
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: sexual violence and torture drawn at the extreme, and the question of whether it is shown for understanding or for shock.

frames_add.aligns: Fate, causality and the gods stay mysterious, the unfinished story gives no final verdict, and sincere faith (Mozgus, Farnese) is shown with some complexity.
frames_add.concerns: Organized religion is shown almost entirely as persecution, which can tip into contempt for believers, and the explicit content needs an adult-level check.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to a small band, protecting the people beside you and refusing to give up are the hope the story offers (v35-41).
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty is often unpunished and the betrayer is rewarded (Griffith, Falconia), and the despair and sexual violence (v13) put it at adult level.

frames_add.aligns: A Klan lynching condemned (ch. 39-41), a Black protagonist and a mother who followed Martin Luther King Jr., and heroes who shield children.
frames_add.concerns: Jesus is shown drawing the bat when asked what God looks like (ch. 14-17), placing a morally ambiguous spirit behind sacred history; a speaking spirit and a cult around it.

frames_add.aligns: Hidden powers that claim to guide history, including the bat itself, are distrusted; human responsibility for stories is the point.
frames_add.concerns: Popular conspiracy theories and real tragedies (JFK, 9/11) used as plot may blur fiction and history.

frames_add.aligns: The bat's nature, God or devil, is left open and the choice is handed to humans (Zeal's Corner).
frames_add.concerns: A reworked account of Jesus may trouble believing relatives; conspiracy material.

frames_add.aligns: Protecting the innocent, and a hopeful last scene in which a child vows to study and save the world.
frames_add.concerns: A ruined future and a dark mood; spiritual manipulation by an unseen power.

frames_add.aligns: Traffickers and adults who prey on children are exposed and punished (circus arc, ch. 24-37; ch. 140), and the wages of a pact with evil are never in doubt (Romans 6:23).
frames_add.concerns: A demon is the admired protector, the hero denies God at the summoning (ch. 136-137) and lives for revenge against Romans 12:19; sexual abuse of ten-year-old twins by a cult is depicted non-explicitly (ch. 135-136) and the child lead is at times drawn in a sexualized way.

frames_add.aligns: Cults, blind faith and aristocratic impunity are exposed, and Ciel works as a reasoning detective; the demons and reapers are fiction.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty and child exploitation are at times drawn for effect, revenge goes unexamined, sexual abuse of children appears (ch. 135-136), and Ciel's unbelief is presented as a wound tied to his damnation (ch. 136-137).

frames_add.aligns: The story raises hard questions about justice, revenge and identity (Ciel taking his brother's name) without forcing an answer.
frames_add.concerns: Glamorized revenge, a demon presented as elegant and loyal, child abuse (ch. 135-136) and a cult leader's control make it heavy, with little room for hope.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty of the household of rescued servants and Elizabeth's devotion are honored, and those who harm children get their payback.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty and revenge are central, the ending is a soul owed to a demon with no way out, and the abuse of children in ch. 135-136 is well beyond a young reader's age.

frames_add.aligns: The lowly are lifted up: an orphan from the Forsaken Realm, raised in a church, overcomes a caste system by birth and reconciles with former enemies (ch. 1-5, 214, 392), in the spirit of James 2:1-9.
frames_add.concerns: The hero's power comes from a devil he befriends and fuses with (ch. 268-273, 326-327), which Holiness and Pentecostal families may see as spiritually real; a running gag of proposing to a nun who refuses.

frames_add.aligns: Worth is earned by effort and character rather than birth, and the devils, angels and magic stay fantasy furniture rather than doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: Little on belief; deaths are often reversed, which can blunt consequences.

frames_add.aligns: A warm church sits beside a mixed spirit world without any one faith presented as the answer, and the villain's 'holy war' warns against a self-proclaimed savior (ch. 331-389).
frames_add.concerns: Holy imagery given only to the villain may feel one-sided to some readers.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to a found family of misfits, fairness for the looked-down-on, and an underdog who never gives up.
frames_add.concerns: Steady battle violence, light fan service and the nun proposal gag may need age judgment (Common Sense Media says 13+).

frames_add.aligns: Revenge is shown to breed more suffering (Romans 12:19), compassion even for enemies is the heroine's defining trait, and cruelty and sexual violence are framed as evil.
frames_add.concerns: The rape of a boy by the villain Shira (likely act 160), a 16-year-old heroine stripped and bound (acts 156-167), repeated rape of adult women, torture and dismemberment; an immortality curse from a nun's bloodworms.

frames_add.aligns: Human compassion is the moral center, no god resolves suffering, and the state's cruel experiments and blind loyalty are exposed (acts 99-134).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual violence, including the abuse of a boy (likely act 160), and cruelty presented as spectacle.

frames_add.aligns: Questions about atonement, meaning in an endless life and whether harm can be balanced are posed honestly and left open.
frames_add.concerns: The abuse of a boy (likely act 160), the stripping of a 16-year-old (acts 156-167), and extreme gore.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty between protector and protected, a sadist who meets a terrible end (acts 167-169), and survivors who find family after loss.
frames_add.concerns: Some of the most violent content in print, with sexual violence against women and a boy (likely act 160) and the deaths of most of the cast.

frames_add.aligns: Endurance through a hostile world, protection of the helpless and a hope handed on through a new child at the end (Logs 64-65), with no evil made attractive.
frames_add.concerns: No God appears and the only religion shown is a destructive cult (prequel); minds are copied between bodies, Killy ends a suffering woman's life (Log 36), and the gore and body horror are constant (Philippians 4:8).

frames_add.aligns: Everything has a natural or technological cause, science and persistence are the only tools, and human life is treated as worth restoring in an indifferent universe.
frames_add.concerns: The bleak tone and the mercy killing (Log 36) call for discussion.

frames_add.aligns: The story explains almost nothing and leaves the big questions (what a person is, what the remote Authority is) for the reader to wonder about.
frames_add.concerns: Constant violence and body horror; the mercy killing.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty between unlikely allies (Killy, Cibo, Sanakan) and a hopeful ending in which a child is protected by water and plants (Log 65).
frames_add.concerns: A mood of isolation and decay close to despair, graphic violence from the first chapter, where a child is killed, and grotesque body horror.

frames_add.aligns: Courage and loyalty protect the weak, an unjust death sentence is defied (vols. 8-20), and blood-purity ideology that kills the weak and mixed-blood is shown as evil (ch. 537, 603).
frames_add.concerns: The premise is traffic with the dead, spirits and death gods, with reincarnation and a sealed 'god' (Hebrews 9:27), God's Hebrew name is given to the villain (ch. 565), and Nazi-era imagery is used for spectacle.

frames_add.aligns: Would-be gods are exposed as power structures (ch. 421, 621), human choices decide the outcome, and Aizen's last word is that fear of death gives hope and courage their meaning (likely ch. 685).
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: violence as the default answer and Mayuri's cruelty partly played for fun.

frames_add.aligns: Questions about who should rule over souls and whether Soul Society's past was justified are raised and honestly left open.
frames_add.concerns: The detailed afterlife system is fiction but firm, and the trans-coded sadistic villain (Giselle, from ch. 544) and Nazi motifs deserve a conversation.

frames_add.aligns: Protecting family and friends, a mother's sacrifice, souls that live on after death, and an ending in marriage and family (ch. 686) fit this tradition's spiritual-but-open outlook.
frames_add.concerns: Long stretches of violence and an institution that keeps its crimes hidden (ch. 46, 621) need discussion.

frames_add.aligns: Hidden sin comes to light (vol. 9, Luke 8:17), the harm a parent does to a child is shown as harm (Ephesians 6:4), and the son's late care for his failing mother (vol. 17) echoes honoring a parent who failed.
frames_add.concerns: No hope beyond a quiet release is offered; the story contains a killing (vol. 12), a long suicide plan (vols. 14-15), incestuous undertones between mother and son, and a sexual scene between two 14-year-olds (likely vol. 5).

frames_add.aligns: The story looks for causes (the mother's own unloved childhood, vols. 15-16) rather than blame or supernatural answers, and a self is rebuilt by human understanding alone.
frames_add.concerns: Sustained psychological abuse, incestuous undertones, a sexual scene between two 14-year-olds (likely vol. 5) and suicide planning shown at length.

frames_add.aligns: The story refuses easy answers, keeps sympathy for both mother and son without excusing her, and leaves the final dream conversation (vol. 17) open to the reader.
frames_add.concerns: The dread, the killing, the sexual content involving minors and the suicide plan make it adult or older-teen reading.

frames_add.aligns: Harm passed from parent to child is finally seen and allowed to stop, and the son chooses to care for his aging mother to the end (vol. 17).
frames_add.concerns: Long stretches of emptiness and despair (vols. 13-14), the killing of a cousin, and disturbing sexual undertones, including a sexual scene between two 14-year-olds.

frames_add.aligns: Honesty in place of a false front, healing from grief over a lost sister (ch. 21-31), loyal friendship and grace in rejection (Sayaka, ch. 37-38).
frames_add.concerns: The story presents a same-sex romance between two high-school girls as the good outcome, which most large Black denominations teach against though members' views vary, and it includes a sexual encounter between the two high-school students (ch. 44) outside marriage (1 Thessalonians 4:3).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is found in honest human relationships, identity is chosen rather than imposed, and no supernatural claims are made.
frames_add.concerns: Touko kisses Yuu repeatedly without asking early on (from ch. 2), and the teens have little adult support.

frames_add.aligns: The story asks who a person really is and lets several answers stand (the play, ch. 30-31), and characters with different experiences of love, including Maki, who feels no attraction, are treated with respect.
frames_add.concerns: Consent in Touko's early kisses; critics still debate how Yuu's orientation was handled.

frames_add.aligns: Finding your own path instead of living as someone else (Touko and her sister), loyal friendship and kindness in rejection.
frames_add.concerns: A sexual encounter between the two high-school girls (ch. 44), and the couple keeps the relationship from Yuu's parents.

frames_add.aligns: Discipline, honest dealing with a rival (ch. 77), gratitude to a host family and endurance after a crushing loss (ch. 133-134) are honored, in the spirit of Philippians 4:8.
frames_add.concerns: A teen couple hides their relationship from the parents they live with for months (ch. 103-156), against Ephesians 6:1-3.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning comes from effort, honesty and choosing your own path, with no supernatural claims.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond secrecy from parents.

frames_add.aligns: A gentle, honest coming-of-age story that respects every character, including the rejected Hina.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise.

frames_add.aligns: Hard work, kindness to rivals, loyalty to friends and a family that takes in a girl from abroad make a warm, decent story.
frames_add.concerns: A relationship kept secret from parents for months, and a slow, restrained teen romance.

frames_add.aligns: A foster father's self-giving love (ch. 1-2), a son who rejects Satan's evil, and prejudice by blood condemned; a woman scapegoated as a witch is shown as wronged.
frames_add.concerns: Scripture used like a spell, demon pacts and a hero who carries Satan's power; the ch. 77 scene of coerced sexual contact involving 15-year-old Yukio; several suicide attempts.

frames_add.aligns: Identity is chosen, not inherited; dogma, cover-ups and unethical science are all critiqued, and no god appears to fix things.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide attempts (ch. 2, 77, 93) and the ch. 77 scene involving a minor; frequent fantasy violence.

frames_add.aligns: Christian, Buddhist and Shinto practice are shown side by side without one declared true; each being is judged one by one.
frames_add.concerns: The ch. 77 scene and the suicide attempts; scripture borrowed as game mechanics.

frames_add.aligns: Chosen family, loyalty between brothers and acceptance of outsiders; spirits and demons can be good or bad.
frames_add.concerns: Possession and occult horror; the ch. 77 scene; suicide attempts.

frames_add.aligns: Honesty, loyalty between old friends, Toma's self-sacrifice (ch. 12), and gossip and exposure shown as harm (Proverbs 16:28).
frames_add.concerns: The story treats same-sex attraction as normal and ends with two men married (Final Chapter), a concern for many families though not all; teen dating.

frames_add.aligns: Identity accepted rather than imposed, honest relationships and no supernatural claims.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise.

frames_add.aligns: Characters work out who they are without anyone handing them the answer; the choices made at eighteen are not final.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the pain of exposure.

frames_add.aligns: Friendship that survives hurt and lasts into adulthood; kindness to the excluded.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; views on the ending vary.

frames_add.aligns: Hard work, discipline, honest self-improvement and using one's gifts fully are honored, and cheating is condemned before the cheater is given a second chance (ch. 18-25).
frames_add.concerns: Selfish ambition is the story's thesis, against Philippians 2:3; the eliminated players are discarded with little care for the weak; and the English edition uses the f-word and God's name often (Exodus 20:7).

frames_add.aligns: Isagi wins by analysis and self-knowledge rather than fate or faith, and tradition and authority are questioned (ch. 1).
frames_add.concerns: Harsh treatment of teenagers (lifetime bans, humiliation) is justified by results, and the dignity of those who lose is ignored.

frames_add.aligns: Self-knowledge and honest analysis of one's own limits are valued, and later arcs soften rivals into partners.
frames_add.concerns: A charismatic leader running a locked facility is vindicated and his thesis is preached in direct speeches, with the opposing view voiced mostly by players who are cut, which runs against intellectual humility.

frames_add.aligns: Effort, fairness on the field and finding your own path are rewarded, and cheating is shown as wrong.
frames_add.concerns: Friendship comes second to ego (Nagi leaves Reo), a controlling institution is celebrated, and the English edition's profanity is frequent.

frames_add.aligns: Gifts developed through disciplined work and education (Colossians 3:23), a teacher who widens a student's world, and a father's violence toward Yuka shown as wrong (likely ch. 17-22).
frames_add.concerns: Casual teen smoking and drinking early (ch. 1-2), nude figure study (v5) and a sympathetic gender-nonconforming, bisexual character that many, though not all, of these families will want to talk through.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is chosen and built through human effort, skill and friendship, with no supernatural claims and religion present only as art history.
frames_add.concerns: Casual teen smoking and drinking and mental-health strain with little help-seeking shown.

frames_add.aligns: The series lets the mother, rivals and professors make real counterpoints and avoids prescribing a takeaway, leaving readers to decide.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise in message; Yuka's despair (likely ch. 6-9) merits a talk.

frames_add.aligns: Finding your own path, hard work, loyal friends and a grandmother who stands by Yuka (v4-5).
frames_add.concerns: Teen smoking, heavy drinking and crude talk in early chapters (ch. 1-2) and nonsexual nudity (v5) may be beyond younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: An abused, trafficked child is adopted into a family (ch. 24-27; James 1:27), a son learns to honor his father (Ephesians 6:1-3), and Boruto stays faithful while falsely accused.
frames_add.concerns: Possession by god-like beings and a curse mark; cover art posing 12-year-old girls in a sexualized way (ch. 13, 19 and 80 covers); frequent ninja violence.

frames_add.aligns: God-like beings are shown as alien predators and people defeat them through cooperation, not worship.
frames_add.concerns: Destiny and bloodline power cut against self-made achievement; the sexualized covers of child characters are a harm concern.

frames_add.aligns: Questions of fate and identity (ch. 79-80, 'The Singularity of Fate') are left open, and no faith is pushed.
frames_add.concerns: Cover art of child characters; violence; the story leans on inherited destiny.

frames_add.aligns: Family loyalty, an adopted son welcomed, and a hero who keeps doing right when everyone believes a lie about him.
frames_add.concerns: Sexualized covers of child characters, possession and devouring tree-beings (Two Blue Vortex ch. 19-21).

frames_add.aligns: Exposes adults who abuse their power over a child and punishes the teacher and the killer, and the boy chooses life over death at the end (vol. 18), in the spirit of Deuteronomy 30:19.
frames_add.concerns: No faith, prayer or church appears as help, the suicide legend is told romantically, and sex between adults and minors (vol. 1-3) is drawn with allure as well as blame, a heavy concern under Philippians 4:8.

frames_add.aligns: A this-life story in which freedom comes from telling the truth and leaving harmful ties, with no supernatural rescue (vol. 17-18).
frames_add.concerns: Exploitation of minors is shown repeatedly and sometimes with allure, and the suicide legend and method run against safe-messaging guidance.

frames_add.aligns: Takes no side on religion and lets an honest confrontation, not any doctrine, resolve the story (vol. 18).
frames_add.concerns: The romantic framing of the double-suicide legend and the allure given to adult-minor sex (vol. 1-3) blur the story's own verdict.

frames_add.aligns: Finding your own path away from a family and town that use you, and choosing to live, are rewarded (vol. 18).
frames_add.concerns: Long stretches of despair and cruelty, an attempted rape that is never addressed, and sexual content involving minors make this adult reading.

frames_add.aligns: Outcasts are taken in and given second chances: an abused orphan learns he has worth, and a child assassin is forgiven and welcomed (ch. 9-17), with a found family much like a church family.
frames_add.concerns: The lead's suicide attempts are played as jokes from ch. 1, an adult's attraction to young girls is a running gag (ch. 30, 37), gangsters are glamorized, and the villain speaks of God's will while using people.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is found in human bonds and problems are solved by reason and deduction, while a zealot's 'purification' of sinful humanity is shown as a cover for control (ch. 46).
frames_add.concerns: Suicide played for laughs works against mental-health care, and an adult's attraction to young girls is treated as comedy.

frames_add.aligns: Characters search for a reason to live without being handed one, and the villain's certainty about sin and God is what the heroes resist.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide humor and the predatory running gag; heavy losses in recent chapters (ch. 117-118).

frames_add.aligns: Found family, loyalty and second chances for people others threw away.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide played as a joke, gangster glamour, and the deaths of beloved characters in recent chapters (ch. 117-118).

frames_add.aligns: Revenge is given up (Anko; Romans 12:19), manipulative 'love' that cuts a boy off from family is shown as destructive (Kiku and Mahiru, v16-18), and love matures into faithfulness across years apart (ch. 200).
frames_add.concerns: A 14-year-old's truancy and night wandering are framed as freedom with no parent or elder stepping in (Ephesians 6:1-4), his bond with an adult-aged vampire drawn as a teenager is sexually coded (from ch. 1), blood-drinking is romanticized, drinking and smoking are casual, and a teenager chooses to die with his lover (v16-18).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is found by choice and relationship with no supernatural rule, depression and loneliness are taken seriously, and revenge gives way to understanding (Anko).
frames_add.concerns: A sexually coded bond between an adult-aged vampire and a 14-year-old boy (from ch. 1), and no adult steps in for a truant, sleepless child.

frames_add.aligns: The story raises honest questions about what makes a life satisfying, treats outsiders and different kinds of love with respect (Seri, Kyoko), and preaches no answer.
frames_add.concerns: The age and power gap in the central romance, and a teenager's choice to die with Kiku (v16-18).

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, finding your own path, letting go of revenge, and a love that stays faithful through years apart (ch. 200).
frames_add.concerns: Truancy and sneaking out at night made appealing, frequent sex jokes and a sexually coded bond with a 14-year-old, and casual drinking and smoking.

frames_add.aligns: Yuuki's humble service, courage and search for his sister are praised, and a secret bureau that experiments on people is condemned.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual contact outside any commitment is the story's built-in reward for work (from ch. 1), with collar-and-chain dominance as the power source, against Matthew 5:28 and Philippians 4:8; beings calling themselves gods rule the underworld.

frames_add.aligns: The dignity of former humans is defended against a state that experiments on them, and Yuuki is a decent, hardworking lead.
frames_add.concerns: Consent is played for comedy: the master's body must pay the reward whether she wishes or not, and Himari agrees to a power without knowing its effects (around ch. 18).

frames_add.aligns: The monsters turn out partly to be victims, and the story gives the Thunder Gods a real grievance.
frames_add.concerns: Women's bodies are centered for the male lead's desire, and the gender-reversed premise is dropped rather than explored.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to the squad, family devotion and protecting the weak are rewarded.
frames_add.concerns: An 18+ series whose payoff is sexual contact; an 11-year-old scout takes part in the reward system with cheek kisses (ch. 25), kept non-sexual according to the entry.

frames_add.aligns: Deliverance from bondage runs through the story: a boy in debt slavery is freed, and Makima's control is exposed and ended (ch. 1, ch. 84-97), echoing Exodus and Luke 4:18.
frames_add.concerns: Devil contracts and Hell are normal and the hero is fused with a devil; lust as a motive, minors drinking (ch. 21), cannibalism called love (ch. 96-97), and no hope beyond human care.

frames_add.aligns: No god rescues anyone; meaning comes from friends, a shared meal and choosing your own wants (ch. 97, 232), and the hero cult around Chainsaw Man is shown as manipulation (ch. 140).
frames_add.concerns: Exploitation and consent problems in Part 2 (ch. 132, 136, 167-168) and heavy cruelty, judged by harm rather than by belief.

frames_add.aligns: The story preaches no answer about God or meaning and ends on an open restart (ch. 232), leaving readers to decide what Denji's life amounts to.
frames_add.concerns: Long stretches of loss without payoff can read as despair, and sexual content involving teens needs an age check.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, an ordinary home and food on the table are the reward, and lost friends return at the end (Power and Nayuta, ch. 232).
frames_add.concerns: Gore, crude sexual content with teen characters and a very bleak middle (ch. 79-82, 150-170) are beyond many children's age.

frames_add.aligns: Genocide and tyranny are shown as evil (ch. 49), the weak are protected, and Tokio shows mercy to enemies (Matthew 5:44) with his father's blessing (ch. 35).
frames_add.concerns: Power comes from an injected drug, visions and marks are shown as real spiritual forces, and there is fan service and heavy body horror; Philippians 4:8 is a fair test.

frames_add.aligns: Goodness comes from empathy and choice, and a vision of the future used to justify killing is shown as dangerous (ch. 49).
frames_add.concerns: Body horror and cruelty; drug-made power is framed as fantasy, so its real-world harm is worth a talk.

frames_add.aligns: Prophecy and fate are left as open, troubling questions, and a charismatic 'Mother' who demands loyalty is shown as dangerous.
frames_add.concerns: Biblical phrases in chapter titles are used without explanation; the unfinished story may still settle these questions.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friendship, a supportive father (ch. 35) and finding your own path, with controlling groups (Zora's tower) shown as harmful.
frames_add.concerns: Gore, body horror, fan service and a drug storyline (v7-8).

frames_add.aligns: A teacher who preys on a student is exposed and removed (ch. 2), a girl who blackmails others repents (likely ch. 12), and the leads wait until 18 to marry (ch. 41).
frames_add.concerns: Forced kissing, groping and a forced undressing between 16-year-old stepsisters (ch. 1, 3), an adult teacher kissing a 16-year-old (ch. 1) and a 14-year-old earning money from adult men (likely ch. 9-12) are part of the story, with the coercion between the leads little corrected; the affirmed same-sex romance differs from the official teaching of most of these churches, a concern for many families but not all.

frames_add.aligns: Personal choice wins over an imposed arranged marriage and family control (ch. 36-41), and the teacher's misconduct is exposed.
frames_add.concerns: Repeated sexual coercion between minors is framed as the start of a romance (ch. 1-12), and fan service of 16-year-olds.

frames_add.aligns: Honest confession resolves what silence and control created (ch. 16, 41).
frames_add.concerns: Force presented as romantic between 16-year-olds (ch. 1, 3), a 14-year-old's paid contact with adult men (likely ch. 9-12), and little adult support.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal devotion, families that come around and reconcile, and a controlling grandfather who bends (ch. 41).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual coercion and fan service involving 14- to 16-year-olds (ch. 1-12) is not age-appropriate, and the step-sibling setting troubles many families.

frames_add.aligns: Women used as weapons by a lying power expose it and are set free (sc. 79-80, v22), outcasts stand together, and a church learns to welcome those it feared and cares for orphans (Rabona, sc. 74-80).
frames_add.concerns: The black card treats killing a friend on request as mercy, Clare is driven by revenge (Romans 12:19), the heroines carry demon flesh and are called witches, a spirit of the dead fights in the finale (v27), and uncensored nudity and sexual threat appear (v3, v23).

frames_add.aligns: Miria investigates and exposes an authority that lies about where the monsters come from, the monsters have a man-made cause, and meaning comes from human bonds and choice.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty, torture and body horror are shown at length, and the mercy-killing pact needs a mental-health conversation.

frames_add.aligns: A fictional church is shown as fearful at first and later hospitable, neither mocked nor declared true, and Teresa's spirit in the finale leaves the question of what survives death open.
frames_add.concerns: Constant graphic violence and a pact that treats assisted death as a duty between friends.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to comrades and to the dead, protection by a loved one's spirit (Teresa, v27), and the fall of an institution that controls people's lives.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic violence, body horror, uncensored nudity and the black card's mercy killing make it a series for older teens.

frames_add.aligns: Calling back the dead is the root evil (ch. 3); mercy for enemies (Matthew 5:44); church leaders who abuse children are confronted, as the prophets confronted unjust rulers.
frames_add.concerns: Souls of the dead trapped and tormented, possession by Nea, Noah recast as the villains' ancestor and God's character left ambiguous; fan service and a reported hint of child abuse (ch. 232, to verify).

frames_add.aligns: Accepting death, empathy for enemies and a hero who leaves an institution that lies; religious authority that hides crimes is exposed.
frames_add.concerns: Self-harm content (ch. 222 and a reported attempt) needs careful framing; body horror.

frames_add.aligns: God's power is real in the story but God's character stays an open question, and faith and the institution are kept apart.
frames_add.concerns: Gore and possession; the series is unfinished, so its final answer is unknown.

frames_add.aligns: Grief carried with hope ('keep walking'), loyalty to friends as home, and an institution that controls people shown as the danger.
frames_add.concerns: Tormented souls of the dead and constant loss; body horror; fan service.

frames_add.aligns: The bullied are defended, a grieving mother's ghost is shown compassion, and adults who prey on teens and a family that sacrifices children are held to account (ch. 28-50; v20-22).
frames_add.concerns: Medium practice, talismans and exorcism are the heroine's family calling and shown as good (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), and teen characters face repeated attempted sexual assault (ch. 1, 33), teen nudity (ch. 20) and constant genital humor.

frames_add.aligns: Kindness and loyalty drive the heroes, religion used to harm or deceive is condemned (the Kito family, ch. 28-50; a fake priest, v24), and spirits are clearly story material.
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: repeated sexual threat aimed at teens (ch. 1, 33), teen nudity, and a teacher blackmailing a student over lewd photos (v20-22), which critics say is used too often.

frames_add.aligns: A believer and a skeptic each mock the other's belief and are both proven wrong (ch. 1), and the story treats mystery with wonder and respect rather than doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: The sexual content involving teen characters and the suicide backstories (ch. 16, 45-49; v18) put it at Mature level.

frames_add.aligns: Spirits are real and helped to pass on, a grandmother's wisdom protects the young, and loyalty, kindness and a found family of misfits are the heart of the story.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual threats against teens, nudity, crude humor and suicide backstories call for an age check (Mature, 15+).

frames_add.aligns: A prophetic critique of rulers and media who turn fear into hatred of a helpless people (Amos 5:24); compassion for the stranger.
frames_add.concerns: Premarital sex and a former teacher's relationship with his student; a child's suicide in another timeline; no hope beyond one human bond.

frames_add.aligns: Critical thinking about propaganda, meaning found in human bonds and no supernatural claims.
frames_add.concerns: Despair and a child's suicide need careful framing; the teacher relationship.

frames_add.aligns: Distrust of anyone who claims final answers, from governments to activists; the ending stays open.
frames_add.concerns: The teacher relationship and young-looking character art.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty between two friends and fairness to a scapegoated people; institutions that control people are the danger.
frames_add.concerns: A pessimistic mood, mass death and a child's suicide in another timeline.

frames_add.aligns: A wrongly convicted boy, prisoners treated as people, a for-profit prison exposed, and mercy chosen over revenge at the end (ch. 57) echo the call to remember those in prison (Hebrews 13:3) and Romans 12:19.
frames_add.concerns: Gore that reviewers call the main draw, heavy profanity, several suicides, and fan service involving teenage girls (ch. 9, 18, 43); no faith or hope beyond this life appears.

frames_add.aligns: Compassion keeps the inmates human, unethical science and profit from suffering are condemned, and the ending chooses life (ch. 57).
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty as spectacle, and sexualized depiction of teenage girls, including a nude scene with an adult touching her (ch. 43).

frames_add.aligns: Labels like 'criminal' are questioned, and a cult-like 'death as salvation' creed is shown as madness (ch. 20).
frames_add.concerns: Extreme gore, sexual-abuse backstories (ch. 9, 20), and several suicides needing mental-health framing.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends who become family, a hero who refuses to kill, and a hopeful epilogue reward fairness and second chances.
frames_add.concerns: Torture, organ removal and a massacre on the page, self-cutting used as a power trigger, and fan service involving minors.

frames_add.aligns: The wages of sin are shown (Galatians 6:7): a boy who profits from selling death dies at the moment he succeeds; greed and a lying ruler are exposed.
frames_add.concerns: No hope or way out is offered; death gods set the rules; a cynical tone with no one standing for what is right.

frames_add.aligns: No supernatural rescue; reason and planning shown with their limits; satire of power and of people hailing a killer as a god.
frames_add.concerns: The rules are changed at will by a supernatural ruler, which undercuts the reasoning.

frames_add.aligns: Satire without preaching; the crowd's quick return to worshiping Kira invites questions about certainty and belief.
frames_add.concerns: A bleak, ironic ending with no answer offered.

frames_add.aligns: What goes around comes around: the clever seller pays for his scheme; greed and power are mocked.
frames_add.concerns: Bleak and cynical; nobody in the story is a model to follow.

frames_add.aligns: A proud man who makes himself 'god of the new world' and judge of life and death is exposed and brought down (ch. 103-107), honoring Romans 12:19, while an honest father and lawful authority stand as the moral center.
frames_add.concerns: No repentance or grace, a closing rule that all the dead go to nothingness (ch. 107), death gods, coerced suicides (ch. 14), and a Kira cult that outlives him (ch. 108).

frames_add.aligns: Reason, evidence and due process defeat a killer, and religious language belongs to the villain and his cult rather than the heroes.
frames_add.concerns: Light's glamor leads many readers to side with him.

frames_add.aligns: Both sides argue for justice and the reader is left to weigh them; a man demanding worship is shown as dangerous.
frames_add.concerns: The story closes the afterlife question with a firm rule of nothingness for all (ch. 107), certainty some agnostic families would rather leave open.

frames_add.aligns: What goes around comes around: Light's choices return on him, and loyalty and honesty (Soichiro, the task force) outlast him.
frames_add.concerns: 'No heaven or hell' may jar with families who believe in an afterlife; coerced suicides and a steady body count (Common Sense Media: 15+).

frames_add.aligns: A brother goes back for his sister, strangers and enemies share meals, gratitude and no waste are taught, and a demon of endless appetite is defeated.
frames_add.concerns: Forbidden black magic raises the dead out of love (ch. 27) and a wish-granting demon speaks in dreams (ch. 60), which Holiness and Pentecostal families may see as spiritually real (Deuteronomy 18:10-12).
