frames_add.aligns: Curiosity, empirical study of an ecosystem and practical reason save the day, magic works like a craft with rules, and mortality is accepted rather than defeated.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; some species stereotypes are used for jokes (orcs).

frames_add.aligns: Big questions about life, death, desire and what we owe what we eat are raised openly and left for the reader to weigh (ch. 51, 93-97).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond body horror in the chimera chapters (ch. 37-38).

frames_add.aligns: Family loyalty, friendship across races, a sister brought back, and a final feast with former enemies reward everyday decency and hope.
frames_add.concerns: Body horror and the cannibalism debate (ch. 51) may unsettle younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Clear good and evil, the strong protecting the weak, honor to parents and elders (Ephesians 6:1-3), mercy toward the repentant and a costly hope that the next generation will live in peace (ch. 205).
frames_add.concerns: Buddhist and Shinto spirits, hell and rebirth are shown as real and the hero's family honors a fire god (John 14:6), Kagaya's self-destruction is framed as heroic (ch. 138), and Holiness families may be wary of literal demons.

frames_add.aligns: The heroes act from human compassion and choice, Kagaya argues human thoughts endure beyond the body (ch. 137), and a cult leader who exploits believers is exposed (ch. 160-163).
frames_add.concerns: The one character who says there is no heaven, god or buddha is the emptiest villain (Doma, ch. 163), and suicide-adjacent sacrifice is framed as heroic (ch. 57, 138).

frames_add.aligns: Afterlife meetings and the rebirth epilogue are offered as quiet wonder rather than doctrine, and the story humanizes its enemies instead of demonizing them.
frames_add.concerns: Self-sacrifice that edges toward suicide (ch. 57, 138, 143) needs a conversation with younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Family loyalty, keeping promises, karma-like justice, the dead watching over and welcoming the living (ch. 66, 156, 200) and a peaceful ending fit this tradition closely.
frames_add.concerns: Constant graphic violence and the heroic framing of Kagaya's and Shinobu's self-destruction (ch. 138, 143) call for an age check.

frames_add.aligns: Stalking, attempted assault and media exploitation of a victim are condemned; self-sacrifice and hard work at a calling are honored.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual scenes involving under-18 characters (ch. 1; vol. 6) and an adult teacher's secret relationship with her 17-year-old student are framed as love and end in marriage; drinking.

frames_add.aligns: Realistic consequences for secrecy (Hina loses her job, ch. 58-64) and meaning made through work and art.
frames_add.concerns: An adult's relationship with a minor student is treated as forbidden love; sexual scenes involving under-18 characters; consent questions (the couch scene, ch. 2-4).

frames_add.aligns: No preaching either way; characters grow through loss, work and friendship.
frames_add.concerns: Power and consent between a teacher and her 17-year-old student; sexual scenes involving under-18 characters.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, sacrifice and friends who rescue each other (Momo's arc) are shown as good.
frames_add.concerns: The 18+ sexual content, including scenes involving under-18 characters; the teacher-student relationship rewarded with marriage.

frames_add.aligns: A mocked boy grows in courage, and a lie is confessed, apologized for and forgiven (vol. 20).
frames_add.concerns: Humiliation and unwanted sexual touching are played as affection in early arcs (ch. 1 onward), sexual content involving high school characters runs throughout, including nude modeling (likely vol. 15), and the story ends with a plan to live together unmarried (ch. 154).

frames_add.aligns: Growth comes from the characters' own effort, honesty and art, and the vol. 20 lie has real consequences that are repaired by apology.
frames_add.concerns: Early arcs frame humiliation and unwanted touching as flirting, a consent problem, and the art sexualizes minors, including nude modeling (likely vol. 15).

frames_add.aligns: Both leads drop their defenses and learn honest communication by the final volume.
frames_add.concerns: The story never questions its early teasing-as-love framing, and the sexualized depiction of high school characters (vol. 1-6, likely vol. 15) is the main issue.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends who become matchmakers, a shy boy finding courage, and honesty and apology valued (vol. 20).
frames_add.concerns: Mockery as humor and sexual content involving minors, including nude modeling (likely vol. 15), are beyond what most families find age-appropriate.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty between friends, hospitality around a shared meal, old enemies forgiven, and a cruel devil ruler humbled at the end (ch. 166-167).
frames_add.concerns: Devils and Hell run the world and becoming a devil is shown as a reward (ch. 155, 167); inverted crosses as decoration; killing played as comedy and revenge as the main justice.

frames_add.aligns: No god or supernatural order is presented as true; friendship, work and humor are what make life good.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty and killing are often played for laughs with little reflection on the harm.

frames_add.aligns: Devils and magic are absurd story machinery, and the series claims no answers about what lies beyond.
frames_add.concerns: Extreme violence treated lightly.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to your crew, a reopened family restaurant and old enemies making peace (ch. 167).
frames_add.concerns: Extreme gore played as comedy and a drug trade, rated 17+ by Common Sense Media and Mature by VIZ.

frames_add.aligns: Education and hard work lift a whole people, the sick are healed (ch. 40-43), a purge of the 'unworthy' and a tyrant's harem are condemned (ch. 4-6, 101-137), and a father's love carries across generations (ch. 44-45).
frames_add.concerns: A world with no God where human knowledge is the only savior, revival nudity, the Treasure Island harem arc, and teens brewing and drinking alcohol.

frames_add.aligns: Every mystery gets a natural explanation, 'sorcery' becomes chemistry (ch. 17-19), reason and shared knowledge save everyone, and the village tradition is explained without contempt.
frames_add.concerns: Chemistry projects that would be dangerous to copy at home.

frames_add.aligns: Curiosity and humility are central: the writer says the more you understand, the more you see you do not understand, and the priestess and her tradition are honored.
frames_add.concerns: The story closes every mystery with a natural answer, which some agnostic families may find leaves little room for wonder.

frames_add.aligns: Teamwork, fairness, loyalty to family and a father who watches over his son through the tales he left behind.
frames_add.concerns: Light fan service and teens making alcohol (Common Sense Media: 13+).

frames_add.aligns: Courage in protecting the weak, a father rising to save his kidnapped daughter (ch. 93-99), and a people's genocide named as evil and reckoned with (ch. 69).
frames_add.concerns: Many gods, angels and a sorcerer are the real order of the world, against the exclusive claim of John 14:6, and fighting is enjoyed for its own sake; Holiness families may weigh the sorcery (ch. 43-67) more heavily.

frames_add.aligns: Mortals' training and invention, not divine favor, win out, and a god who wants to erase mortals is defeated (ch. 17-26).
frames_add.concerns: An all-powerful ruler who erases universes on a whim is never questioned (ch. 26, 34), and violence is played as fun.

frames_add.aligns: Gods are characters with flaws rather than objects of worship, and the story preaches no doctrine either way.
frames_add.concerns: Absolute power without moral reason is accepted as the shape of the cosmos (ch. 42).

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to family and friends, former enemies given a seat at the table, and Android 17's selfless wish restoring every universe (ch. 42).
frames_add.concerns: Constant fighting as the answer to problems; the revived Frieza goes largely unpunished.

frames_add.aligns: Perseverance, loyalty, mercy to defeated enemies and the redemption of rivals such as Piccolo and Vegeta, who lay down their lives for others (ch. 467), are honored.
frames_add.concerns: Many gods, a demon king and resurrection by wish are the real order of the world, which Holiness families may weigh as spiritually real, and lechery and nudity gags in vols. 1-16 go unpunished, against Philippians 4:8.

frames_add.aligns: Effort and invention, not divine help, decide outcomes, and gods are characters who can be out-trained rather than worshiped.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual gags without consent, including a child removing a sleeping teen girl's underwear and nudity of the child hero (ch. 2, 4, vols. 1-16), are played as harmless; fighting is enjoyed for its own sake.

frames_add.aligns: A playful mix of gods, afterlife and rebirth is offered as folklore rather than doctrine, and former enemies are always given a way back.
frames_add.concerns: Harassment played for comedy and every arc settled by greater power.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, second chances for rivals, the dead who still watch over and help the living, and a villain reborn as a good boy (ch. 517-519) reward hope.
frames_add.concerns: Roshi's lechery and early nudity gags (vols. 1-16), drinking for laughs, and mass violence in the later arcs.

frames_add.aligns: The guild acts like a church family that bears one another's burdens (Ephesians 4:2-3), welcomes repentant former enemies, and frees the enslaved children of the Tower of Heaven (v10-12).
frames_add.concerns: Spirit contracts, demons made from books and a ghost founder are the world's power, constant fan service plays women's bodies for laughs, and drinking is a guild pastime.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning comes from human bonds, no gods are worshiped by the heroes, and former enemies earn second chances through their own choices.
frames_add.concerns: Conflicts are settled by force and power-ups more than reasoning, and women are sexualized as running gags, including forced stripping (v33).

frames_add.aligns: Accepts eccentrics and outsiders of every kind and preaches no doctrine; gods and spirits are fantasy setting.
frames_add.concerns: Fan service and harassment played as comedy undercut the respect the story preaches.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends who become family, forgiveness, and a dead founder who still watches over the guild (Tenrou, v28-30) are what the story rewards.
frames_add.concerns: Heavy fan service and casual heavy drinking (Cana) are the main age questions.

frames_add.aligns: Hope defeats despair, heroes protect people who call them devils, a church that uses faith to control people is exposed (ch. 123-130) in the prophetic spirit of Amos 5:24, and the sincere faith of Sister Iris is honored.
frames_add.concerns: Powers come from communion with an evil being ('Grace') and an otherworld (Adolla), a human becomes a creator who makes Death (ch. 300-301), a priest is a fanatic killer of children (ch. 22-33), and Tamaki's sexual-humiliation gags recur, with profanity in the English text.

frames_add.aligns: A state church used to spread fatalism and control is exposed, and Benimaru argues that people should do right for its own sake, not for gods.
frames_add.concerns: The finale resolves everything through a god-like hero, and the recurring sexual-humiliation gags around Tamaki treat harassment as comedy.

frames_add.aligns: Sincere belief (Iris) and doubt (Hibana, Benimaru) are both given dignity, while the institution that demands unquestioning faith falls.
frames_add.concerns: The ending settles the big questions with a cosmic re-creation, and the fan-service gags draw criticism from reviewers.

frames_add.aligns: Hope over despair, a team that becomes a family, a church and empire that control people brought down, and an ending in which the dead are revived and death is feared less.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic horror of people burning, including children's deaths mentioned, and repeated gags built on a young woman's humiliation.

frames_add.aligns: Slavery and trafficking in Behemdorg are condemned and freed slaves are protected, and revenge is shown destroying the avenger (vol. 1-5; compare Romans 12:19).
frames_add.concerns: Religion appears only as human invention and crowd control, with a man worshipped as god and no true God (vol. 4, 8); pervasive sexual violence, including sexual exploitation of children (vol. 1-2); incest themes (ch. 1, vol. 6-7); suicide attempts and a despairing tone.

frames_add.aligns: Gods and myths (the Ice Witch, the Agnist cult) are exposed as human inventions used to control crowds, and meaning is something chosen.
frames_add.concerns: Long, cruel depictions of exploitation, including of children, and a bleak view of human nature.

frames_add.aligns: Sun's sincere devotion is pitied rather than mocked, and the ending leaves the meaning of a life as an open image (vol. 8).
frames_add.concerns: Belief is shown almost only as manipulation and fanaticism, a certainty in one direction; sexual violence used heavily as backdrop.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to a sister and to a found family (Togata), and the command to 'live on' even in pain.
frames_add.concerns: Rated Mature: constant violence, sexual abuse, self-harm and a nihilistic cosmic ending that many families will find beyond a teen's age.

frames_add.aligns: A faithful marriage built on daily care and a husband who works hard and cherishes his wife (Ephesians 5:25); despair answered by love (ch. 146-148).
frames_add.concerns: Bath, sauna and towel scenes with a bride who looks 16, sexual jokes from a 15-year-old side character, a marriage made after one meeting, and an elixir-of-immortality myth.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning built through love and work; Nasa treats the elixir as a problem for reason (ch. 268, 279).
frames_add.concerns: Haste of the marriage and the wife's long secret.

frames_add.aligns: Big questions about endless life and death are left open with curiosity.
frames_add.concerns: Haste, secrecy and some fan service.

frames_add.aligns: Family blessing, loyalty and a chosen family across generations (Tokiko's will); a gentle folk myth.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond mild fan service and the teen marriage premise.

frames_add.aligns: Hard work, learning and serving ordinary people are honored, and students stand up to an abusive father and a controlling regime and win (Central arc, ch. 135-263).
frames_add.concerns: Sexualized 'foodgasm' reactions of high-school characters are played as comedy throughout (from ch. 1-5), and the epilogue sets up a half-sibling marriage plot (Le dessert).

frames_add.aligns: Experiment, curiosity and learning from failure beat one enforced 'true' standard imposed from above.
frames_add.concerns: Sexualized reactions of teenage characters as comedy; late sympathy for an abusive father.

frames_add.aligns: No one is allowed to impose one 'correct' taste on everyone, and rivals with different views are learned from rather than mocked.
frames_add.concerns: Fan service involving teenage characters and the half-sibling plot in the epilogue.

frames_add.aligns: Hard work, friendly rivalry, a found family in the dorm, and a broken family reconciled.
frames_add.concerns: Frequent fan service involving high-school characters; an abusive father given late sympathy.

frames_add.aligns: A family held in bondage by fear is set free (ch. 115-132), sacrificial kindness and endurance through grief carry the story, and the abuser is given a road to repentance (ch. 132).
frames_add.concerns: Nudity of named minors when they change back (ch. 14, 61), a past sexual relationship between two minors (ch. 79), and a romance between a middle-school girl and an adult trainee teacher framed as rescue (ch. 90-92); spirit possession by zodiac animals.

frames_add.aligns: The family's god turns out to be a wounded, controlling human, and healing comes from people accepting one another, not from worship (ch. 131-132).
frames_add.concerns: The content-warning items involving minors (ch. 14, 61, 79, 90-92) and heavy abuse for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: The legend behind the curse is shown as a lonely being's demand, and characters reach their own conclusions about forgiveness (Rin, ch. 132).
frames_add.concerns: The adult-minor romance (ch. 90-92) is framed as romantic rescue; nudity and sexual history involving minors (ch. 14, 61, 79).

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, everyday kindness, a mother remembered as watching over her daughter, and a controlling family institution dismantled so each person finds their own path (ch. 132-136).
frames_add.concerns: The content-warning items involving minors (ch. 14, 61, 79, 90-92), a parent's suicide (ch. 34) and the abuse scenes.

frames_add.aligns: Racism and genocide against the Ishvalans are condemned, the persecuted people are restored to their holy land (v27), a fraudulent preacher is exposed (ch. 1-2), and pride that would make itself God is cast down (ch. 104-108; Isaiah 14:13-15).
frames_add.concerns: Truth is a non-Christian god figure, alchemy binds souls to armor and Stones, which Holiness families may read as occult, and Edward's skepticism about God is never answered.

frames_add.aligns: Evidence exposes Cornello's fake miracles (ch. 1-2), the dead cannot be brought back, and humans fix their world by their own effort and responsibility.
frames_add.concerns: A godlike Truth is real within the story and science without ethics is shown as dangerous; strong violence and the chimera (ch. 5) need age care.

frames_add.aligns: Religion is shown fairly in several forms (a fraud exposed, a sincere persecuted faith honored, a mysterious Truth), and doubt is not punished.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise in message; the violence and body horror are the main issue for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Brotherly loyalty, hard work, a karma-like rule that nothing comes free, a father's redemption and a hopeful ending where the brothers give more than they take (v27).
frames_add.concerns: Frequent gore, Nina's chimera (ch. 5) and the Ishvalan war (ch. 57-61) are beyond many younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: A boy despised for his birth and falsely condemned (ch. 1) proves his worth, the lowly are lifted up and the wasteful rich are judged (Luke 1:52), and the abuse of a child is shown as evil (Amo's arc).
frames_add.concerns: Revenge is the hero's early aim (Romans 12:19), objects carry soul-like power (Anima), profanity is frequent, and Amo's backstory includes the trafficking and sexual abuse of a child, shown indirectly (likely ch. 38-43); the creator faced a 2026 controversy over a racially insensitive fan video.

frames_add.aligns: Human worth does not depend on birth, hereditary guilt and rushed executions are condemned (ch. 1), and the heroes solve problems by their own effort, repair and teamwork.
frames_add.concerns: Rudo's revenge drive and frequent gory fights.

frames_add.aligns: Compassion for outcasts and fellow victims (Rudo and Amo) is grounded in empathy, and the soul-like Anima of cherished objects is left as a mystery of the world rather than a doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: Anger and revenge drive much of the early plot, and the series is ongoing, so its final verdict is unknown.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to a found family (the Cleaners), gratitude to a foster father (Regto), fairness for those treated as trash, and the sense that cherished things carry something of the people who loved them.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic violence, coarse language, and Amo's backstory of child trafficking and sexual abuse (likely ch. 38-43), shown indirectly.

frames_add.aligns: Kato dies saving a stranger nobody else would help and lays down his life for his little brother and others (ch. 1; John 15:13), and bystander indifference is shown as wrong.
frames_add.concerns: Frequent explicit nudity, sex and sexual assault (v1-2, v10, v17-25), extreme gore, profanity and slurs, and a final word from god-like beings that there is no God and souls are worthless (ch. 369-370), left unanswered by faith.

frames_add.aligns: Love, courage and altruism are shown to matter in an indifferent universe with no God needed, and the heroes make their own meaning (ch. 376-383).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual violence and objectified women used for spectacle, homophobic jokes, and cruelty shown for shock; the reveal also asserts souls exist.

frames_add.aligns: The heroes live by love without claiming to know the answer to the cosmic questions.
frames_add.concerns: The final arc delivers a confident lecture that God does not exist (ch. 369-370), religion appears only as monsters or helpless prayer, and no believer is shown fairly.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to a brother and to the person you love carries the heroes home (ch. 383).
frames_add.concerns: Extreme gore, explicit sexual content and assault, and a bleak cosmology in which humans are like ants are far beyond what most families find age-appropriate (publisher-rated 18+).

frames_add.aligns: Two girls share their last ration (ch. 2), return goods taken from graves, and keep each other company to the end, a quiet picture of loyalty in a ruined world much like Ecclesiastes.
frames_add.concerns: There is no hope beyond death, religion is called a fairy tale (ch. 10), young teens get drunk (ch. 21 likely), and the ending can be read as a quiet death.

frames_add.aligns: Curiosity, books, art and friendship are what is worth keeping, and religion is discussed as a human comfort people built to face death (ch. 10).
frames_add.concerns: Underage drinking (ch. 21 likely) and a bleak ending for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: The big questions about death, prayer and meaning are asked honestly and left open, including the ambiguous ending (ch. 47).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; Yuuri's mockery of a temple statue may bother some.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friendship, small joys and respect for the dead make the days worth living.
frames_add.concerns: The steady sense that nothing lasts and the possible death at the end may read as hopeless; teen drinking is shown warmly.

frames_add.aligns: Grief carried in community, friends who bear a hurting person's burden (Galatians 6:2), suicide mourned rather than glamorized, and forgiveness after harm.
frames_add.concerns: Same-sex romance presented as the good life, a concern for many families though not all; adult premarital sex; a forced advance (vol. 4) and a sexually charged scene between high-school students (vol. 7).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning made through art and relationships; grief faced honestly without supernatural comfort.
frames_add.concerns: Consent in the vol. 4 and vol. 7 scenes, the second involving minors; suicide content for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Several views of love get a fair hearing, and the story presses no doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: The same consent concerns and suicide content.

frames_add.aligns: Friends and bandmates carry Mafuyu through loss; the dead are remembered with love (Yuki's song).
frames_add.concerns: The vol. 7 scene between high-school students and adult sexual content; suicide content.

frames_add.aligns: Courage and loyalty in protecting forgotten villages; captives rescued and temples caring for survivors (ch. 2); evil is never excused.
frames_add.concerns: Bath scenes involving the 15-year-old Priestess (ch. 20 and later); on-page sexual violence (ch. 1, 44-45); pagan gods and miracles shown as good; a war driven partly by revenge, and goblin children killed (ch. 2).

frames_add.aligns: Competence, study and preparation win; survivors' trauma is treated as real; gods in the setting are fiction and do not count against it.
frames_add.concerns: Fan service around a minor; sexual violence used for shock; an entire race written as beyond redemption.

frames_add.aligns: Priestess is allowed to question the hero's no-mercy rule and he concedes a good goblin could exist (ch. 2).
frames_add.concerns: Graphic sexual violence and a minor in bath scenes; an extermination ethic left mostly unquestioned.

frames_add.aligns: Protecting ordinary people, loyalty to companions, and a lonely man drawn back into a shared life (ch. 42).
frames_add.concerns: Rated 18+: sexual violence, gore and fan service involving a 15-year-old are far beyond a child's age.

frames_add.aligns: A caring adult takes in a child no one else would raise, and beastmen held as a lower class are treated with dignity; compassion for the outcast (Psalm 68:5-6).
frames_add.concerns: Corpses raised as monsters and other-realm gates touch the wariness about spirits; smoking, drinking, a suicide-pact chapter (ch. 19) and mild fan service in a red-light setting.

frames_add.aligns: Humanity is defined by Alma's choices and Tao's care, not by origin or any god (ch. 12); the religious names are setting only.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide content (ch. 19) is raised without mental-health framing; constant monster violence.

frames_add.aligns: Buddhist, Shinto and Taoist names are used as atmosphere without pressing any doctrine; the open question of what makes someone human is left to the reader.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide themes and abuse are raised but, per one reviewer, never explored.

frames_add.aligns: Found family and loyalty are the moral center: Tao raises Alma and the team holds on to him; Kanata is pitied, not hated (ch. 9).
frames_add.concerns: A grim, violent world with smoking, drinking and suicide themes; T+ rating.

frames_add.aligns: An Indigenous girl refuses to let stolen gold fund other men's wars and protects her people's land (ch. 311-314), greed destroys every faction, and Sugimoto keeps his promise to a widow (James 1:27).
frames_add.concerns: Ainu kamuy worship and a seer whose prophecies come true (ch. 122) are shown as real, and extreme gore, profanity and perversion played for laughs (likely ch. 109-113) fail the Philippians 4:8 test.

frames_add.aligns: Skill, reason and human bonds decide survival, war trauma is faced honestly, and the ending chooses land and future over wealth with no supernatural rescue.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty played for laughs, including animal abuse and cannibalism, and a trans woman written as a cannibal villain (likely ch. 50-58).

frames_add.aligns: Ainu belief is shown with respect without being pushed, every faction's grand cause is questioned, and charismatic leaders who demand loyalty (Tsurumi) are shown as dangerous.
frames_add.concerns: Constant gore and comic treatment of atrocities.

frames_add.aligns: Promises kept, gratitude to the animals that feed you, respect for spirits and loyalty among friends reward everyday decency.
frames_add.concerns: Extreme violence, crude sexual humor, serial killers as recurring villains, and Ogata's suicide (likely ch. 310).

frames_add.aligns: Life is chosen twice over despair, a father confesses and apologizes for ignoring his wife's abuse of their son (pp. 118-137; Ephesians 6:4), and a dying friend is cared for to the end.
frames_add.concerns: Two suicide scenes, one with a 12-year-old (pp. 33-41) and one with an adult (likely pp. 172-180), grief met with no hope beyond this life, and the idea that memory may be edited away from the plain truth.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is made through art and relationships, with no supernatural comfort needed, and the story looks honestly at how memory and media shape truth.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide content for younger readers; the fact-or-fiction ambiguity may frustrate some.

frames_add.aligns: The ending deliberately leaves open what is real, and the story invites readers to decide for themselves.
frames_add.concerns: Two suicide scenes need safe-messaging conversations.

frames_add.aligns: A boy keeps his loved ones close through the stories he tells, a father makes amends, and life goes on after loss.
frames_add.concerns: Two suicide scenes and a parent's emotional abuse in a book rated Teen Plus.

frames_add.aligns: The story tells the truth about neglect, abuse and broken homes, condemns adults who harm children, and honors a dying mother's apology and a friend who steps in to save a life.
frames_add.concerns: There is no hope beyond bare survival, God appears only as a comic inner voice, an abortion is planned without judgment (JP v9-10), and suicide, sexual content and the sexual abuse of a high-school boy by an adult (ch. 50) are shown on the page.

frames_add.aligns: Cults are shown as deadly (Mitsuko; the Pegasus group), no supernatural rescue comes, and what keeps a person going is work, time and a few human ties.
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: repeated suicide scenes against safe-messaging guidance, sexual coercion by the protagonist and the abuse of a minor (ch. 50).

frames_add.aligns: The author says the world has many values and none is simply right, the story offers questions rather than answers, and the ending is left open.
frames_add.concerns: Its bleakness and the suicide and abuse scenes make it adult reading.

frames_add.aligns: Everyday decency survives in Sachi's friendship and a mother's late apology, and life goes on for the next generation.
frames_add.concerns: Despair dominates, and suicide (ch. 138-147), abuse of a minor (ch. 50) and sexual content put it well beyond children's age.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends who stand up for a bullied classmate (ch. 9) and try to help her stay in school (ch. 41-44).
frames_add.concerns: Abstinence is widely taught in these churches, and drunkenness and pressure to drink are the main joke (ch. 1-2, 21, 29; Ephesians 5:18), alongside constant censored male nudity and crude sexual gags.

frames_add.aligns: Irreverent comedy, real diving knowledge and a found family with no religious framing.
frames_add.concerns: Coerced binge drinking and alcohol poisoning are played for laughs, involving 18-year-olds in the manga, against evidence on real harm, and refusing a drink is shown as social failure.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty and the shared wonder of the sea are the story's warm center.
frames_add.concerns: The sober view is mostly held by characters who are the butt of jokes, and consent to drinking and stripping is routinely ignored (ch. 1-2, 29).

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, a found family, and fun that is never preachy.
frames_add.concerns: Underage-looking binge drinking, spiked drinks and nudity gags (ch. 1-2, 21, 29) are more than many families want for teens.

frames_add.aligns: A teacher who refuses to give up on any child pulls bullied and suicidal students back from the roof (early volumes) and stands up to a school that sorts children by scores, like the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine (Luke 15:4).
frames_add.concerns: A teacher's lust toward 14-year-old students is a running joke from vol. 1, profanity is constant, and violence and lawbreaking are framed as heroic rather than repented of.

frames_add.aligns: Every student's worth is defended against a system of rank and test scores, and care is shown through action, not doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual humor around minors (from vol. 1), cruelty and corporal punishment played for laughs, and a rape survivor's arc (vol. 21-22) resolved by a male hero's lesson.

frames_add.aligns: Questions every authority that claims to know best, from vice-principals to an administrator who runs the school as a business (vol. 20).
frames_add.concerns: Results excuse reckless and illegal methods, and sexual jokes about students recur throughout.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, keeping your word and standing by kids when institutions fail them are rewarded, and several families reconcile.
frames_add.concerns: Several suicide attempts (vol. 2-3, 16-17, 24-25), sexual content involving minors as comedy, and dangerous stunts presented as fun.

frames_add.aligns: Humility that values others above oneself (Philippians 2:3-4), perseverance after defeat, a teammate who once quit restored to the team (ch. 119-120), and mentors who protect a player's health (ch. 365).
frames_add.concerns: Mild to moderate swearing in English versions, a coach who smokes, adults drinking, and comic ogling of the team manager.

frames_add.aligns: Practice, analysis and teamwork win, and Takeda tells Hinata that some obstacles need knowledge and reason rather than willpower (ch. 365).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise.

frames_add.aligns: Rival teams' philosophies are treated with respect and no worldview is pressed on the reader.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, fair play, learning to lose well, and each player finding his own path after school (ch. 386).
frames_add.concerns: Some swearing and smoking (Common Sense Media: 13+; ScreenWise: 10+).

frames_add.aligns: Perseverance through suffering (Hebrews 12:1), honoring a widowed mother (Ephesians 6:1-3), a bully redeemed and the hero later protecting a bullied boy (ch. 1229-1246).
frames_add.concerns: Takamura's groping and lewd gags (ch. 355-357) and drinking scenes fail the Philippians 4:8 test for some families; Common Sense Media notes some foreign fighters are drawn poorly.

frames_add.aligns: Growth comes from human effort, training and reason, and the CTE scare (ch. 1202-1208) is handled by medical evidence, not miracles.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the sport's risks and crude comedy.

frames_add.aligns: No doctrine pressed either way; kindness, humility and respect for rivals carry the story.
frames_add.concerns: Groping gags played for laughs (ch. 355-357) raise consent questions.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to family and gym, everyday decency, and fair payback: fouls and contempt lose while the bully Umezawa becomes a friend (ch. 506).
frames_add.concerns: Long bloody bouts and the head-injury risk; lewd comedy around adults.

frames_add.aligns: Self-made gods who harvest people and offer a false paradise are exposed and fall (Psalm 115), a husband's faithfulness drives the hero home (ch. 127), and condemned convicts and a persecuted people are treated with dignity.
frames_add.concerns: Taoist energy and sex magic are shown as real power the heroes learn to master; manga nudity and sex scenes; sexual coercion, including of a character shrunk into a child's body (Hōrai arc); extreme gore.

frames_add.aligns: Faked divinity and invented religion used for control are exposed, Senta's study of religions is a tool of reason, and meaning is found in finite human bonds rather than immortality.
frames_add.concerns: Depicted sexual coercion and constant graphic violence need context for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Taoist balance and Buddhist ideas are explored as a world-system and as questions rather than doctrine, and doubt is shown as strength in Sagiri (ch. 120).
frames_add.concerns: Buddhist and Taoist sacred names worn by villains may feel careless toward real traditions.

frames_add.aligns: Love that gives a reason to live, loyalty formed across enemy lines, and fair treatment for outsiders; souls are laid to rest with respect (ch. 15).
frames_add.concerns: Rated Mature (Common Sense Media: 16+) for buckets of blood, body horror and on-page sex.

frames_add.aligns: Lies and vanity lead to ruin, and the yakuza boss's confession and turn from violence (likely JP v3-6) echo repentance.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual activity between a 34-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl is framed ambiguously as a kind of rescue (likely JP v5-8), self-mutilation and a hanging are shown, a 'sixth sense' is gained by drilling the skull, and no hope is offered beyond the self.

frames_add.aligns: Ito's skeptical, scientific frame and the placebo reveal question whether the visions are real, and the supernatural is never confirmed.
frames_add.concerns: Experiments on a person for money are the premise and are not clearly condemned, skull drilling is presented as a door to insight, and a minor's sexual exploitation is framed ambiguously (likely JP v5-8).

frames_add.aligns: The story honestly leaves open whether Nakoshi's visions are real or projections of his own mind.
frames_add.concerns: The sexual scene with a 17-year-old and the death of Nanako (likely JP v13-15) are framed without a clear verdict on the harm done.

frames_add.aligns: One character finds peace by confessing and laying down violence, and a father and son partly reconcile.
frames_add.concerns: Pervasive despair, cruelty to the vulnerable, a suicide by hanging (likely JP v6-8) and sexual content involving a minor make it adult reading with a bleak, nihilistic ending.

frames_add.aligns: A lonely, bullied boy is seen and healed by friends (Psalm 147:3), a teen girl cares for her little brother, a former bully is forgiven, and the romance moves toward marriage (likely vol. 9).
frames_add.concerns: Two high-school students have an implied, off-page first sexual experience that the story does not judge (ch. 37; 1 Corinthians 6:18), Hori's hitting of her boyfriend partly becomes a gag (ch. 42-43), and a self-harm and suicidal-thought flashback (ch. 10) is healed with no adult or church help.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning comes from being known and accepted by other people, with kindness and honesty and no religious framing.
frames_add.concerns: Depression is resolved by love alone with no adult or professional help, and partner violence is sometimes played for laughs (ch. 43).

frames_add.aligns: A quiet, unpreachy story about not judging people by appearance, with customs such as the New Year shrine visit kept lightly (vol. 10).
frames_add.concerns: The self-harm flashback (ch. 10) and the teen sexual relationship (ch. 37) may need a conversation.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends, everyday decency, family care and a hopeful ending in engagement and family fit this tradition well.
frames_add.concerns: An implied sexual relationship between high schoolers (ch. 37), a self-harm flashback (ch. 10) and hitting played as comedy call for an age check.

frames_add.aligns: Human sinfulness is named plainly (ch. 298; Jeremiah 17:9), revenge is shown to destroy the avenger (Romans 12:19), humility defeats pride (Komugi, ch. 242-258), and Killua protects his confined sister.
frames_add.concerns: No side is clearly good, Nen and prayer work as spiritual power sources, violence is often fun, Hisoka shows a sexualized interest in the boy heroes (likely ch. 13-68), and gender-fluid characters are a concern for many but not all families.

frames_add.aligns: Nen is a learnable natural system, meaning is found in chosen bonds rather than given from above (ch. 316-318), and human cruelty is faced honestly with empathy across species.
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: cannibalism and body horror in the Chimera Ant arc and Hisoka's predatory framing.

frames_add.aligns: Even the monsters get a full hearing, the story refuses to name a good side, and its biggest questions (what makes someone human) are left open for the reader.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide in combat (ch. 298) and the violence of the Chimera Ant arc need a conversation.

frames_add.aligns: Friendship that outranks a cruel family (Killua), loyalty, finding your own path, and a quiet gratitude practice (Netero) fit this tradition well.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic violence, body horror and a creepy adult villain (Hisoka) call for an age check.

frames_add.aligns: Sexual slavery, cult violence and tyranny are shown as evil; Hiromi's empathy and Hideo's protection of the weak.
frames_add.concerns: A 35-year-old man's sexual act with a high-school girl (likely vol. 17-18) is framed as a bond; extreme gore; no hope beyond survival.

frames_add.aligns: No supernatural answer; empathy across the human and infected line; religion appears only as a killer's cult.
frames_add.concerns: The adult-minor sexual act is not treated as harm; cruelty for shock.

frames_add.aligns: Leaves the question of what a good life is open, and treats cult certainty as dangerous.
frames_add.concerns: The same adult-minor content; a bleak ending without meaning offered.

frames_add.aligns: Small acts of care and protecting the vulnerable.
frames_add.concerns: Despair and nihilism dominate; an adult's sexual act with a high-school student is framed as a bond; extreme gore.

frames_add.aligns: An abandoned orphan given a family (ch. 22); despair overcome (ch. 1); captives rescued (ch. 92 on); a false god who erases grief is exposed (ch. 23-42).
frames_add.concerns: Witch and magic vocabulary, possession, blood contracts and raised dead (ch. 73), which Holiness and Pentecostal families may weigh heavily (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); the hero's eye-for-an-eye rule.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning chosen after despair (ch. 1); research-minded Witches; a worshiped being that numbs sorrow is shown as harmful; magic is fiction.
frames_add.concerns: Prophecy used as a plot device; the hero's reciprocal killing rule, which the author calls dangerous.

frames_add.aligns: Grief treated as worth keeping; wonder at living magic; no religious claims pressed either way.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the violence and the eye-for-an-eye rule.

frames_add.aligns: Found family, loyalty, protecting the weak and honoring grief; a hopeful spirit throughout.
frames_add.concerns: Monster violence and the undead scenes (ch. 73); a prophecy of the hero's death hangs over the story.

frames_add.aligns: The story sides with the condemned, the poor and the abused against a cruel ruling class (Amos 5:24), and Charles's conscience before God is treated with respect.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual abuse of a 9-year-old girl and a 14-year-old boy is part of the story (vols. 1, 5-6), along with eroticized torture of the teenage hero, nudity and extreme gore, which fail the Philippians 4:8 test.

frames_add.aligns: Medicine, anatomy and reform point the way forward, and the dignity of the condemned rests on shared humanity.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual abuse of minors is part of the plot (vols. 1, 5-6), and critics debate whether the art makes cruelty glamorous rather than examining it.

frames_add.aligns: Charles's faith and Marie-Joseph's rejection of God are both shown seriously, and the story leaves the reader to weigh conscience against duty.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual abuse of minors (vols. 1, 5-6), eroticized torture of a 14-year-old and heavy gore; adult readers only.

frames_add.aligns: Mercy and conscience are the story's moral center, and the corrupt marshal Griffin is executed (vol. 6).
frames_add.concerns: The outlook is bleak, with innocents executed and cruelty mostly unpunished; sexual abuse of minors (vols. 1, 5-6) and graphic torture place it well outside teen reading.

frames_add.aligns: Truth-telling to parents and a turn from a false identity back to the real self; a loyal friend who refuses to give up (Yori).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual scenes involving a 16- or 17-year-old's body, including contact with a 21-year-old man (likely vols. 5-6); masturbation and voyeurism; no faith or hope beyond the self.

frames_add.aligns: The supernatural premise is explained psychologically; healing comes through honesty and friendship.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving a minor's body, even framed as critique; stalking and a forced kiss (vol. 3).

frames_add.aligns: Takes seriously how little we know about selves and minds; no preaching either way.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving a minor's body (likely vols. 5-6); a long portrait of a predatory gaze.

frames_add.aligns: A girl finds her way back to herself, her family returns for her graduation, and a lonely man rebuilds a modest life.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual scenes involving a teenager's body are far beyond a child's age; stalking and a controlling mother.

frames_add.aligns: Hope that endures a heart defect and fear of death; loyalty, study and a promise kept (vol. 14); care for a lonely friend.
frames_add.concerns: Teen dating and the two teens left alone overnight on the summer trip (vol. 6); defying parents (vol. 7); the suicide legend (vol. 1); peace is found in each other, not in God.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning built from friendship, craft and astronomy; the ghost legend is shown to be an invented story (vol. 1); courage before death without a supernatural rescue.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; some will note that romance is close to being shown as the cure for anxiety, with therapy barely raised.

frames_add.aligns: The night sky as wonder without a fixed answer; fear of death faced honestly and humbly; no preaching either way.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the unsupervised trip (vol. 6) and the light treatment of professional help.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, everyday kindness and hope; local festivals and legends kept as warm custom (ch. 13, 54-55); a happy ending earned by effort.
frames_add.concerns: The overnight trip and the grounding that follows (vol. 6-7); the suicide legend needs a word for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Desire left unchecked is shown destroying people (James 1:14-15), predators are punished, and the hero slowly turns from enjoying violence toward protecting others.
frames_add.concerns: Extreme gore, a hero who relishes killing for much of the run, revenge by mutilation, and sexual violence in the plot, including the rape of a 16-year-old character and her childhood abuse by her father (likely v8-12).

frames_add.aligns: Desire, boredom and social pressure are explained in human terms, and the hero's change is his own choice.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty is often played as dark comedy, sexual violence involving a minor is used as shock, and the ending's life-for-life offer needs safe-messaging care.

frames_add.aligns: The story asks honestly what people would do with their real desires and leaves its owl patron and its ending ambiguous.
frames_add.concerns: Extreme gore and sexual violence, including against a 16-year-old character, with little positive vision until late.

frames_add.aligns: Predators get what they deserve and the hero ends up fighting for other people.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty and despair dominate, the ordinary life of marriage and family is framed as dull, and sexual violence involving a minor is part of the plot.

frames_add.aligns: Joseph stands up for Smokey against corrupt police and a racist gangster (ch. 1, 3), friendship crosses race and class, Caesar lays down his life for a friend (ch. 48; John 15:13), and would-be gods fall.
frames_add.concerns: The hero's lying and comic peeping are celebrated (ch. 37; Proverbs 12:22), the gore is heavy, an SS officer becomes a friendly ally, and reviewers note caricatured drawings of the Black character Smokey.

frames_add.aligns: Human wit, training and solidarity defeat beings once worshipped as gods, and the would-be perfect being ends powerless (ch. 65-69).
frames_add.concerns: A prophecy is treated as true (ch. 18), and a Nazi officer who orders prisoners killed is later played as a likable hero (ch. 9, 62, 67).

frames_add.aligns: No preaching; cleverness and humility before a stronger foe win, and the bid for godlike perfection is punished (ch. 69).
frames_add.concerns: Graphic body horror and man-eating (ch. 10-26) and a Nazi regime used as backdrop without judgment.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends and family, a mother found, and payback for the villain who betrayed everyone (ch. 62-69) fit these families' sense of fairness.
frames_add.concerns: Frequent gore and man-eating may be too much for younger readers, and the friendly Nazi ally is worth a talk.

frames_add.aligns: Neighbors, friends and even children stand together against a hidden killer, the murdered girl Reimi gets justice at last (Amos 5:24), and the wicked man is judged (ch. 163-174).
frames_add.concerns: Ghosts and town guardian spirits treated as real (ch. 65-69, 173-174), serial murder and a killer's hand fetish, and sexual crimes against minors stated in text (ch. 3, 55) with a teen girl in a towel (ch. 83-85).

frames_add.aligns: Observation, reasoning and cooperation expose the killer, and goodness is framed as simply not doing harm (Araki); the ghosts are folklore inside the fiction.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic killings (ch. 81, 99), sexual crimes against minors stated in text (ch. 3, 55) and a teen in a towel (ch. 83-85); an obsessive, controlling crush played partly for laughs (ch. 29-37).

frames_add.aligns: A folk-like spirit world with no theology, a ghost who rests once justice is done, and a moral that rests on empathy and community (ch. 174).
frames_add.concerns: Serial murder and gore, stated sexual crimes against minors (ch. 3, 55), and Yukako's possessive love treated partly as comedy.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends and neighbors protect their town, the dead are put to rest, and the killer gets a fitting end (ch. 174), all fitting a sense that what goes around comes around.
frames_add.concerns: A serial killer of women, stated crimes against children in a villain's past (ch. 3) and a teen's sexual thoughts read aloud (ch. 55) push this toward older teens.

frames_add.aligns: A crew that fights the sale of drugs to children, a man who disobeys an evil boss to protect a girl (ch. 78), and friends who give their lives.
frames_add.concerns: Gang life is the heroes' path and the 15-year-old hero ends as a crime boss; constant violence; gags about 15-year-old Trish's body (ch. 47, from ch. 133).

frames_add.aligns: Human loyalty and conscience against a tyrant, with no supernatural moral authority needed.
frames_add.concerns: Fate presented as fixed; vigilante justice; a minor's body played for laughs.

frames_add.aligns: Fate and what lies beyond death are treated as mysteries the characters face with courage.
frames_add.concerns: Heavy violence and gang life as the road to good; the gags about Trish.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends and karma-like justice for Diavolo; the dead watch over the living ('Sleeping Slaves').
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty and gang life admired; the jokes about a 15-year-old girl.

frames_add.aligns: A friend lays down his life for a friend (Josefumi, ch. 53; John 15:13), a mother risks her life for her unborn child (ch. 82), an outsider is adopted into a family, and greed for a cure sold only to the rich ends in death (1 Timothy 6:10).
frames_add.concerns: A family curse is passed on by burying a child alive under a shrine (ch. 64) and broken by an exchange that kills rather than by grace (Galatians 3:13), and the story includes 'evil eye' rituals, uncensored adult nudity, an attempted assault under mind control, and a suicide attempt (ch. 71).

frames_add.aligns: Identity is built by choice and relationships, the family's curse rituals are shown as harmful superstition, and disaster carries no divine meaning (ch. 104).
frames_add.concerns: Heavy violence, uncensored adult nudity and an attempted assault used as a plot twist.

frames_add.aligns: The story asks honest questions about memory, identity and inherited guilt and leaves the curse's spiritual meaning open while ending in hope (ch. 108).
frames_add.concerns: Graphic violence and body horror, and the assault and suicide attempt told briefly.

frames_add.aligns: Found family, gratitude and loyalty, villains who reap what they sow, and a hopeful ending at the family table (ch. 110).
frames_add.concerns: Graphic violence including a child buried alive (ch. 64), adult nudity, and a suicide attempt (ch. 71).

frames_add.aligns: Pride that makes itself a god is brought down (ch. 11, 42), the hero lays down his life for his wife and an orphaned baby (John 15:13; ch. 44), and he mourns even his enemy.
frames_add.concerns: Vampires, zombies, an Aztec sacrificial mask and a prophecy; a crucifix shown as powerless; animal cruelty (ch. 4-5); a Chinese character drawn as a stereotype (ch. 7, 10).

frames_add.aligns: The creator's theme is that humanity is wonderful and people win by courage, learning and friendship without divine help.
frames_add.concerns: Gore and animal cruelty; a prophecy is accepted as true inside the fiction.

frames_add.aligns: A clear moral about pride and courage that pushes no religious answer either way.
frames_add.concerns: Gothic horror and animal cruelty (ch. 4-5); fans' love of the villain is worth discussing.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends across class lines, a father who dies for his son, and the villain's cruelty catching up with him.
frames_add.concerns: Gore, the burning of the dog (ch. 4-5) and the vampire mother scene.

frames_add.aligns: A son and his friends cross the world to save a dying mother, three companions lay down their lives for others (ch. 125-143; John 15:13), and a tyrant who rules by fear is destroyed.
frames_add.concerns: A fortune-teller hero, tarot and Egyptian-god names (Deuteronomy 18:10), heavy gore and animal mutilation, a child's partial nudity and an attempted assault on her in a shower scene (ch. 18), a sister's rape stated in backstory (ch. 14), and stereotyped portraits of Asian, Middle Eastern and dark-skinned characters.

frames_add.aligns: No god acts; human courage, solidarity and Kakyoin's dying deduction defeat Dio, and the tarot names are spectacle rather than a belief the story asks readers to hold.
frames_add.concerns: Gore played for spectacle, the shower scene with a child (ch. 18), women drawn as victims or villains, and cultural stereotypes along the route (ANN).

frames_add.aligns: A wide, curious world of myth and fate used as adventure without preaching, and a would-be god-king who demands worshipful loyalty is destroyed.
frames_add.concerns: Constant graphic violence, the attempted assault on a child (ch. 18) and a dismissive view of the peoples of India and the Middle East.

frames_add.aligns: Family loyalty, friends who give everything for each other and a mother saved, with ghosts and fate treated half-seriously (Iggy's ghost, ch. 132).
frames_add.concerns: Frequent gore and animal deaths, the shower scene with a child (ch. 18) and the stated rape in Polnareff's backstory make it for older teens.

frames_add.aligns: A ruler who uses God's name to make his nation first at others' expense is condemned and falls (ch. 78-89), in the prophetic spirit of Amos 5:24, and a guilt-stricken nun's repentance is treated with sympathy (ch. 56-57).
frames_add.concerns: Christ's body is cut into power-granting relics and he dies again in a distant land (ch. 67), against the Resurrection and Ascension; sexual threats against 14-year-old Lucy (ch. 60-61); Common Sense Media flags the Black racer Pocoloco as a stereotype.

frames_add.aligns: Araki's stated theme is growth 'without relying on machines or gods'; the relics are finally sealed away as belonging to no one, and a ruler's claim of divine favor for his nation is defeated.
frames_add.concerns: The Saint's power and counsel are real inside the story, which some families will want to frame as fiction.

frames_add.aligns: The Corpse is never named and Araki left its identity unclear, treating it as a symbol of purity rather than a doctrine (vol. 24 note).
frames_add.concerns: Graphic violence and body horror; the story's reworking of Jesus may unsettle believing relatives.

frames_add.aligns: A loyal friendship, a son reconciled with his father, and a proud ruler who meets a fitting end.
frames_add.concerns: Constant gunfights, gore, strong language and sexual threats against a minor (Common Sense Media: 14+).

frames_add.aligns: A false shepherd who uses God's name for evil is exposed and defeated (Matthew 7:15-20), a Klan lynching is shown as evil (ch. 128), the falsely imprisoned are defended, and Jolyne lays down her life for a child (ch. 155).
frames_add.concerns: The villain is a priest who calls Christ's cross mere fate (ch. 143) and loves a vampire 'as God' (ch. 94); souls are pulled from bodies; a masturbation reference (ch. 1), sexual subtext involving a 16-year-old (likely ch. 94) and strong profanity.

frames_add.aligns: Human choice, solidarity and hope defeat a cosmic plan sold as Heaven, and a religious leader's claim to know what is best for everyone is exposed (ch. 157).
frames_add.concerns: Constant gore, prison torture and strong language (TV-MA anime).

frames_add.aligns: A man who claims certainty about God's will and fate is the villain, and the story sides with an open, unknown future.
frames_add.concerns: The only developed religious figure is a villain, so believers are not shown from more than one side; heavy violence and sexual material.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty between a father and daughter and a found family of inmates, fate and justice taken seriously, and the friends returning in a new world (ch. 158).
frames_add.concerns: Constant gore, a lynching and a suicide (ch. 128), the heroes' deaths (ch. 152-155) and strong language are well beyond younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: A false religious leader who takes followers' money is defeated (Matthew 7:15), his contempt for ordinary people as 'monkeys' is condemned, and a bullied teen who once tried to die chooses to live for others.
frames_add.concerns: The hero's power is the bound spirit of a dead girl, to whom he offers himself (ch. 0-4), and curses are summoned and absorbed throughout, which Holiness and Pentecostal families read against Deuteronomy 18:10-12; past suicide attempt and heavy gore.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning comes from relationships and chosen purpose, and organized religion appears only as Geto's fraud, exposed and defeated.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide and grief content and graphic violence for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Spirits and curses are used as a way to think about grief and letting go, without preaching any doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: A charismatic supremacist is the villain, and the suicide and violence content needs age care.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends and a protective teacher, love that frees the beloved, and a dead girl who passes on in peace and asks Yuta to live (ch. 0-4).
frames_add.concerns: Gore, a monstrous spirit and a past suicide attempt (likely ch. 0-1) make it older-teen reading.

frames_add.aligns: Yuji keeps choosing to protect the weak after failing (ch. 127 onward), mentors lay down their lives for others (John 15:13), and a corrupt elder council is confronted.
frames_add.concerns: Sorcery, summoning, possession and cursed objects are the heroes' own tools (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), a cult cheers a child's death (ch. 72-76), and suicide appears on page (ch. 113).

frames_add.aligns: No god acts; curses come from human fear and hate, Yuji's ethic rests on human dignity, and the religious group that applauds Riko's death is condemned (ch. 72-76).
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: very heavy violence and suicide content (ch. 113, 117-125) for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Villains get fair, strong arguments, no doctrine is preached, and the afterlife scenes (Nanami, Gojo, ch. 271) are left as open wondering rather than answers.
frames_add.concerns: Frequent sudden deaths of loved characters and a teen's collapse into despair (ch. 127) need an age check.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, helping people and dying without regret are the life message (ch. 1), and the dead appear at peace in afterlife scenes.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic mass death, suicide on page (ch. 113) and long stretches of loss (Shibuya, vol. 13-16) are beyond many children's age.

frames_add.aligns: Human trafficking at the Rakuzaichi auction is condemned and captives are freed (vols. 3-5; Luke 4:18), and propaganda that calls a people 'savages' is exposed as a lie (ch. 72).
frames_add.concerns: Killing his father's murderers is the hero's goal, against 'vengeance is mine' (Romans 12:19); graphic dismemberment in nearly every fight and torture by the hero's mentor.

frames_add.aligns: Evidence overturns an official war myth and the 'enemy' is shown to be human (ch. 72), with no religion invoked to justify anyone.
frames_add.concerns: Revenge drives the plot, conflicts are settled by stronger blades, and the gore is constant.

frames_add.aligns: Villains such as Yura are given partly true causes, and the hero's own inheritance is questioned rather than simply celebrated.
frames_add.concerns: The story has not yet settled whether revenge is right, and violence is the main pleasure on offer.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to a father, a found family (Shiba, Hakuri, Iori), protecting the vulnerable and a sense that wrongs come back on those who do them.
frames_add.concerns: Constant graphic violence, torture and child endangerment (vols. 1-5) are beyond younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Honesty over pride, hard work and education lifting a poor student, a falsely accused outcast restored by friends (ch. 88, 245-246), and a daughter freed from a family that treats her as a tool (ch. 249-261).
frames_add.concerns: The lead couple, both high-school students, have a first night together that is framed as a natural step (ch. 220), sex jokes are frequent (vols. 7-8, 17-18), and deceptive schemes are the comedy's engine (Proverbs 12:22).

frames_add.aligns: Reason, wit and honest relationships carry meaning, religion is incidental, and justice comes to the falsely accused through investigation (ch. 88).
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: sexual jokes about high-school characters and manipulation played as romance in early chapters.

frames_add.aligns: A light, unpreachy comedy about the courage to be honest, with folklore and holidays kept as story rather than doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: Frank sexual talk and the teen couple's first night (ch. 220) may need a conversation.

frames_add.aligns: Friends who become family, fairness to the outcast, honesty and a hopeful ending fit this tradition well.
frames_add.concerns: Frequent sex jokes and the high-school couple's first night (ch. 220) call for an age check in the later volumes.

frames_add.aligns: A humble working man gets a second chance, keeps his word (Ecclesiastes 5:4-5) and uses his strength to protect the weak inside a team that learns to trust him.
frames_add.concerns: Spirits of the dead act in the final chapters (ch. 113, 129) and the hero's monster form is modeled on an oni; frequent bloody monster gore.

frames_add.aligns: Training, science and cooperation defeat monsters treated like natural disasters, and competence beats talent (ch. 1-7).
frames_add.concerns: The climax leans on a ghost restoring Kafka's heart (ch. 129) rather than on human effort alone.

frames_add.aligns: A mostly secular story whose late spirit layer is left as folklore and wonder, with no doctrine attached.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the gore.

frames_add.aligns: Never too late, loyalty to friends and a father's spirit watching over his successor (ch. 129).
frames_add.concerns: Bloody monster gore (the anime is rated MA 15+ in Australia) and a few nudity and toilet gags.

frames_add.aligns: The shunned girl is lifted up by patience and sincerity, slander is defeated (James 3:5-10), friends defend each other (v2), and both fathers are honored and won over rather than defied (v12, v18, v27).
frames_add.concerns: Teen dating culture, overnight stays (ch. 113-114) and, after graduation, the 18-year-old couple sleeping together off-page (ch. 122).

frames_add.aligns: Rumors about Sawako's 'curses' are disproved by plain experience, and meaning comes from honest relationships and chosen work (v1-v2, v19-30).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; the gender roles are conventional and the final volume's off-page intimacy (ch. 122) is a family conversation.

frames_add.aligns: Kindness and honest words reach people across misunderstanding, and even the manipulator Kurumi is allowed to change (v11, ch. 120); no one is preached at.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the slow pace and the off-page sexual relationship after graduation (ch. 122).

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends, loving parents, fairness to the outsider and New Year shrine visits kept as family custom (ch. 113-115) fit everyday decency.
frames_add.concerns: Mild: teen romance throughout and the couple's off-page night together once both are 18 (ch. 122).

frames_add.aligns: A war orphan rises from servitude by courage and loyalty, and the heroes protect civilians and spare prisoners against Huan Yi's massacres (v41-44, v62-64).
frames_add.concerns: Peace is sought by conquest rather than the beating of swords into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4), revenge and glory drive many fighters, the atrocity-committing general is the fans' favorite, and the Queen Dowager scenes (v34-40) add sexual content.

frames_add.aligns: No god guides history; law, reason, merit and the king's faith in human goodness build order (v39-40).
frames_add.concerns: Ends-justify-means reasoning for years of war and large-scale cruelty that readers find attractive in Huan Yi.

frames_add.aligns: Rival visions of how to rule (Lü Buwei's wealth, Li Mu's balance of states) get serious hearings rather than mockery.
frames_add.concerns: A charismatic autocrat who demands total loyalty is idealized and the story never doubts its goal of unification by conquest.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to comrades, rising from nothing, keeping promises to the dead and fair treatment of prisoners and civilians.
frames_add.concerns: Constant battlefield violence and massacres (v41-44, v62-64) are well beyond younger readers, and a cruel general is presented with strong appeal.

frames_add.aligns: Patient kindness toward a frightened, overlooked girl, a church-family kind of belonging in the class, and an honest, chaste romance (ch. 301-305).
frames_add.concerns: Fan-service gags and lewd jokes about schoolgirls; Najimi's undefined gender as a running gag, a concern for many families though not all; Yamai's kidnapping forgiven quickly (ch. 23-26).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning comes from human connection and patient effort, and the 'Church of Komi' fans gently mock worshipping a person instead of knowing her.
frames_add.concerns: A real anxiety condition is handled by friends alone, with no adult or professional help shown.

frames_add.aligns: Open-minded acceptance of many different kinds of people, with no worldview pressed on the reader.
frames_add.concerns: Some gags at the expense of difference (Najimi, Yamai) may undercut that openness.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, everyday decency and a gentle, hopeful story about finding your place.
frames_add.concerns: Fan-service camera angles and lewd jokes that Common Sense Media flags at 13+.

frames_add.aligns: Noticing the overlooked person (1 Samuel 16:7), kindness to a lost child and an elderly stranger (ch. 134-138), and a slow, chaste romance with no kiss.
frames_add.concerns: Mild fan service with high-school characters (ch. 2, 49-50, 82-85); an adult's drinking at a picnic (ch. 30-31); teen dating as a family decision.

frames_add.aligns: Human connection gives life meaning; confidence grows through friends and family, with no supernatural framing.
frames_add.concerns: Teasing that sometimes pushes past Shiraishi's discomfort.

frames_add.aligns: Gentle and humane; shrine and temple visits are shown as sightseeing without any claim.
frames_add.concerns: Teasing and boundaries; mild fan service.

frames_add.aligns: Everyday decency, friends who cheer each other on, warm family life (Seita, Yoshie).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond mild fan service and the teasing debate.

frames_add.aligns: Pride and manipulation are shown ruining a community (ch. 80-97), and the 'useless' gem is treated as someone who matters.
frames_add.concerns: Salvation is extinction prayed by a human-made god (ch. 95-97), set against John 14:6, and despair, a suicide attempt (likely v6) and an ending without hope beyond nothingness run against the tradition's call to endure in hope.

frames_add.aligns: Empathy for every kind of being is the story's core value, and its religious machinery is built by humans and openly questioned.
frames_add.concerns: Prayer literally works as the world's resolution within the story (ch. 97), and the despair and suicide-attempt scenes need care for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: The story enacts a religious answer and then questions it, leaving the reader to judge whether release into nothingness is salvation or loss.
frames_add.concerns: Its bleak ending (v12-13) and the suicide attempt (likely v6) may weigh on younger or vulnerable readers.

frames_add.aligns: Souls, prayer and a hidden order to the world are taken seriously, and loyalty among friends and a teacher's patient love are honored.
frames_add.concerns: Long stretches of despair, a suicide attempt and an ending in which every soul is erased (ch. 97-108) offer little of the hope or reunion these families tend to look for.

frames_add.aligns: Players are freed from debt bondage again and again, greed and predatory lending are condemned (1 Timothy 6:10), a manipulative cult leader is exposed and repents (ch. 149-169), and a dictator-admirer loses.
frames_add.concerns: Gambling is the premise and lying is taught as strategy (Proverbs 12:22); a mother's suicide in Akiyama's backstory; the trans character Fukunaga is a concern for many families but not all.

frames_add.aligns: Reason, game theory and trust built on understanding win, a demon-bloodline cult is exposed as cold reading (ch. 103-169), and the ending opposes censorship.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; the only religion shown is a fraud, which some may find one-sided.

frames_add.aligns: A charismatic leader who demands belief is unmasked, and Akiyama's idea that to trust someone you must first doubt them prizes honest inquiry (ch. 200).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the suicide backstory (likely ch. 17-18).

frames_add.aligns: Fairness and care for losers, enemies forgiven (ch. 6-7), and controlling institutions, from a cult to a dictator, beaten by players who trust each other.
frames_add.concerns: Detailed cons and bluffing could be imitated; the suicide in Akiyama's past.

frames_add.aligns: Envy is outgrown into friendship (Galatians 5:26), gifts are used for others, a lonely classmate is drawn out with kindness, and grief after senseless violence is told honestly and leads back to faithful work.
frames_add.concerns: No faith or hope of resurrection is shown, the voice of the dead friend and the strip that crosses timelines are left ambiguous (likely pp. 125-140), and the attacker in the first published version was coded as mentally ill (since revised).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is made by people through friendship and work in a world without guarantees, and the ending makes no supernatural claim it presents as fact.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; the mass killing and survivor's guilt call for a conversation.

frames_add.aligns: The story leaves open whether the alternate timeline and the friend's voice are real, a dream or memory, and invites the reader to wonder without insisting either way.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; the sudden violence of the last third can be hard for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friendship, gratitude, a sense that the dead friend still reaches the living, and the choice to keep going after loss.
frames_add.concerns: A mass killing at an art school, mostly reported rather than shown, and Fujino's self-blame.

frames_add.aligns: Bondrewd's use of children as material is shown as evil, and the children's loyalty and sacrifice for one another (ch. 23-38) echo John 15:13.
frames_add.concerns: No hope beyond this world, a mercy killing left without verdict (likely ch. 24), heavy gore, and child nudity that reviewers call sexualized (vol. 1, vol. 11-12).

frames_add.aligns: Curiosity, wonder and the ethics of research are taken seriously, and goodness comes from the children's own compassion (Nanachi, Reg) in an indifferent world.
frames_add.concerns: Extreme cruelty to children, and reviewers' charge that child characters are drawn and exposed in sexualized ways (vol. 1, vol. 11-12).

frames_add.aligns: Leaves hard questions open, such as euthanasia (Mitty, ch. 23-24) and what is worth any price, and gives even the villain a coherent voice.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty to children and the sexualized framing of child characters that reviewers criticize (vol. 1, vol. 11-12).

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty among friends, Riko's search for her mother, and mercy for the suffering carry the children through.
frames_add.concerns: A bleak, indifferent world, cannibalism of infants (ch. 50), heavy body horror, and child nudity that reviewers find sexualized.

frames_add.aligns: Deliverance from slavery is the heart of the story: Morgiana freed (ch. 1-17), slavery and caste condemned, and the poor of Balbadd given a voice, an Exodus pattern.
frames_add.concerns: The heroes' power comes from spirits named after the 72 demons of an occult grimoire, King David is recast as the final villain, and groping gags are played for laughs.

frames_add.aligns: The god-like system that writes 'fate' is ended and people govern themselves by reason and choice (ch. 351-369).
frames_add.concerns: Groping gags and fan service as comedy; little in the message itself.

frames_add.aligns: Rival visions of order (Kou, Magnostadt, Sinbad) get a fair hearing before the story chooses freedom, and the life-flow of the rukh is left as wonder rather than doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: Groping and fan service early on; the story takes a firm line against any guided destiny.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends, fairness that catches up with the cruel, the dead returning to a shared flow of life, and institutions that control people defeated.
frames_add.concerns: Groping gags and fan service; war and genocide in the Magnostadt arc (ch. 160-199).

frames_add.aligns: Misaki works hard to carry her mother and sister through debt (Colossians 3:23), stands up for weaker students and against predators, welcomes home a father who left (ch. 69), and the story ends in marriage (ch. 85).
frames_add.concerns: Two attempted sexual assaults on the 16-year-old heroine (ch. 3, 8), stopped and condemned; Usui's forceful kisses presented as romantic (ch. 4, 18; 1 Corinthians 13:5); the maid café setting.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning through honest work, responsibility and chosen relationships, and a girl who enforces equal rules in a boys' school; no supernatural framing.
frames_add.concerns: Consent is blurred in the romance (forceful first kiss, ch. 4; Tora's forced kiss, ch. 80), and the attempted assaults on a minor (ch. 3, 8) are hard reading.

frames_add.aligns: No preaching; critics and the story both leave room to debate whether it challenges or reinforces gender roles, and money that tries to buy people loses (ch. 8).
frames_add.concerns: The attempted assaults (ch. 3, 8) and pushy romance played as charming (ch. 4, 18).

frames_add.aligns: Hard work, loyalty to family and friends, and fairness between boys and girls are rewarded, and a returning father is given a second chance (ch. 69).
frames_add.concerns: The two attempted assaults in the first volumes (ch. 3, 8) and the forceful kisses are worth a talk for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Hope and endurance through grief, a household that takes in an orphan like a church family, and Hinata's stand against bullying at real cost (ch. 52-73), in the spirit of Micah 6:8.
frames_add.concerns: An adult affair, the bar setting and drinking forced on the underage Rei (likely ch. 3), and Rei's marriage declaration to a first-year high school girl (ch. 104).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is built through human relationships and honest work, and depression is met with care and, for Chiho, treatment.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; the age gap in the romance (ch. 104, 171) is worth discussing.

frames_add.aligns: Rei's questions about why he lives are taken seriously without a doctrinal answer, and people who did wrong, like Kyoko, are given depth (ch. 139).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the drinking and the age gap in the romance.

frames_add.aligns: Family loyalty, everyday decency, a dead mother and grandmother honored at home, and a selfish father who gets his due (vols. 10-11).
frames_add.concerns: Underage drinking (likely ch. 3) and the timing of Rei's romance with Hinata (ch. 104, 171).

frames_add.aligns: An eight-year revenge plan collapses once the truth comes out, and the one who lied confesses, works to repair the harm and is forgiven (ch. 38-49), in line with Romans 12:19.
frames_add.concerns: Fan service with 16-17-year-olds, including a running gag that one girl wears no underwear (likely ch. 8) and swimsuit scenes (ch. 13-15); mocking nicknames and fat-shaming played for laughs (Ephesians 4:29).

frames_add.aligns: Checking what really happened overturns a false belief, and honest talk settles the conflict (ch. 38).
frames_add.concerns: Humiliation humor and fan service of minors (likely ch. 8, ch. 13-15); body-image pressure.

frames_add.aligns: A grudge held as certain truth turns out to rest on a story no one checked, a fair lesson in humility.
frames_add.concerns: Fan service involving high-school characters (likely ch. 8, ch. 13-15) and cruelty as comedy.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friendships survive, a wrong is owned and forgiven, and love wins over payback (ch. 49).
frames_add.concerns: Fan service of 16-17-year-olds is not age-appropriate for the 13+ readership, and fat-shaming and humiliation are played for laughs.

frames_add.aligns: A society that ranks people by a mark they are born with and kills the 'unfit' is shown as wrong and ends, an adoptive father's love saves a rejected child (ch. 1), and a man who tries to become a god falls while the humble hero forgives him (ch. 155-161).
frames_add.concerns: Wand magic and spells fill every page, which Holiness and Pentecostal families may weigh, elites use 'a gift from God' to justify ranking people (likely ch. 46), and Regro's near-suicide is told in ch. 1.

frames_add.aligns: Worth comes from character and effort, not inherited gifts, and the elites' claim that magic is 'a gift from God' that justifies their rank is exposed.
frames_add.concerns: The near-suicide backstory (ch. 1) needs careful framing.

frames_add.aligns: A light comedy that questions inherited certainties about who counts, with a humble hero who claims no special truth.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond slapstick violence and a thin female cast.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to family, kindness, hard work, simple contentment (cream puffs) and fairness for people others call worthless.
frames_add.concerns: Comic violence and a brief near-suicide backstory.

frames_add.aligns: Kindness between strangers, a young man who protects a woman from drunk men without taking advantage, and a chaste night (likely ch. 7-8).
frames_add.concerns: Two nude images of the 17-year-old heroine (front pages and likely ch. 4-6), her smoking and drinking without comment, and an evolution-centered origin story many families do not share.

frames_add.aligns: Life's history is told as evolution from the first cell, and meaning is found in human attention and memory rather than in gods.
frames_add.concerns: Nude images of a 17-year-old (front pages, likely ch. 4-6) and normalized teen smoking and drinking.

frames_add.aligns: The book wonders at deep time and what one life means without giving a final answer, and its ending leaves the mystery open.
