frames_add.concerns: Nude images of a 17-year-old (front pages, likely ch. 4-6); the heroine is seen mostly through a young man's eyes.

frames_add.aligns: A brief meeting that is never forgotten and a sense that every life is part of a much larger story.
frames_add.concerns: A 17-year-old smokes and drinks throughout, and two nude images of her appear (front pages, likely ch. 4-6).

frames_add.aligns: Quiet courage, loyalty to a friend, a self-sacrifice for another (ch. 37), and parental abuse and animal cruelty shown as wrong (ch. 21-23).
frames_add.concerns: Spirits of the dead, genuine mediums and a bargain with shrine gods are the premise (Deuteronomy 18:10-12), and the early chapters frame high-school girls sexually, including a bath scene (ch. 1-17, ch. 7).

frames_add.aligns: Several hauntings turn out to be rooted in human cruelty and grief, and kindness and self-control carry the story.
frames_add.concerns: Real-world folk practices (salt, charms, mediums) are shown working and skeptics are simply wrong; early sexualized framing of teenage girls.

frames_add.aligns: The story keeps its monsters and gods unexplained and morally mixed, leaving room for wonder without a doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: The camera's focus on teenage girls in the early chapters; constant horror imagery.

frames_add.aligns: A dead father still honored at the family table (ch. 9), friends who share the burden, and suffering spirits released.
frames_add.concerns: Sexualized framing of high-school girls early on, constant dread, and sinister shrine gods who demand a price (v4-6).

frames_add.aligns: Humility, honesty and love of enemies win; bullies and boasters are humbled and given second chances (Teru, Ritsu), and a liar confesses (ch. 99-100).
frames_add.concerns: Spirits, possession and lay exorcism are real in the story and psychic power is a neutral gift, which Holiness and Pentecostal families weigh heavily; a suicide in Mogami's backstory (ch. 62-65).

frames_add.aligns: Fake psychics are exposed, cults that demand worship are mocked (ch. 5-9, 91-97), and worth comes from how you treat people, not from special powers.
frames_add.concerns: Spirits are real inside the fiction, which does not lower the grade; Reigen's exploitation of a child is long played for laughs.

frames_add.aligns: The story exposes manipulative leaders without sneering at belief itself, and spirits are part of the world without any doctrine being pushed.
frames_add.concerns: The Mogami arc's torment and bullying (ch. 59-67) are heavy.

frames_add.aligns: Kindness, honest effort and loyalty between brothers, with a spirit world taken half-seriously and controlling groups defeated.
frames_add.concerns: The Mogami arc (ch. 59-67) and its backstory suicide; smoking and a scamming mentor.

frames_add.aligns: A hero who will not take vengeance (Romans 12:19) and treats a migrant worker, orphans and even his enemy as equally worth saving, while racist arson against Turkish neighbors is condemned (v3-4).
frames_add.concerns: Many suicides and suicide games driven by the villain, heavy drinking and long dread, with hope that is human rather than explicitly from God.

frames_add.aligns: The equal worth of every life is grounded in empathy and medicine rather than command, and the story refuses the villain's nihilism without any supernatural answer.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; the Antichrist motif stays a thriller device.

frames_add.aligns: The open ending (the empty bed, ch. 162) leaves the nature of evil unresolved, and both Christian and secular readings are left available.
frames_add.concerns: A magnetic nihilist villain may draw admiration a family will want to talk through.

frames_add.aligns: Everyday decency, fairness and loyalty win out over despair, and many characters (Eva, Lunge) get second chances.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide content, child abuse and psychological dread put it at 15+ (Common Sense Media).

frames_add.aligns: Honesty, care for each other and Jiro's self-control when tempted (ch. 8-12; ANN ep. 5) are rewarded, and the story points toward marriage and family (finale shrine walk).
frames_add.concerns: High school students living together as 'spouses' modeled as normal, constant fan service of a high-school girl, and jokes mocking virginity, against Hebrews 13:4 and 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5.

frames_add.aligns: No supernatural frame; love is learned through honest self-knowledge and shared work, and Jiro will not take advantage of Akari (ANN ep. 5).
frames_add.concerns: Fan service focused on a high-school character, blurred consent in the teasing scenes (anime ep. 4-5), and a school system that grades students' intimate lives without question.

frames_add.aligns: Gentle and pro-social with no preaching; both girls are treated fairly and the ending is left open (ANN ep. 12).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual teasing and fan service involving high school seniors, and the 'Orwellian' graded marriage accepted rather than questioned.

frames_add.aligns: Showing up, telling the truth and choosing the person who really knows you; a romance shrine as part of everyday life.
frames_add.concerns: Rated 16+ by retailers: frequent fan service of high-school characters and sex jokes may be beyond younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: A wasted life given a second chance, a father and son reconciled (v7), and prejudice against the Superd people condemned through Ruijerd (v3-4).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving child and teen characters, much of it played as comedy (v1-2; ch. 51), with those harmed forgiving without repair; plural marriage; a spirit-being guiding the hero through dreams.

frames_add.aligns: The only 'god' who speaks turns out to be a manipulator, and Rudeus grows by study and effort without divine help.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving minors and consent violations are treated lightly, and legal slavery goes unexamined (v13-14).

frames_add.aligns: The story questions a voice from above that helps for its own ends and leaves rebirth as a premise, not a doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving child and teen characters played for laughs; the hero's harm to others gets little moral weight.

frames_add.aligns: Family loyalty, a scattered family searched for and rebuilt, and a real second chance.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving child and teen characters is played as comedy in the early volumes (v1-2), and slavery is shrugged off.

frames_add.aligns: Abuse is named as evil, a friend's love is honored, a stranger's kindness pulls the heroine back from the cliff, and she protects a girl being chased (likely ch. 4).
frames_add.concerns: A father's sexual abuse of his daughter as a child and teen is stated in dialogue and flashback (likely ch. 1-3); suicide and self-harm, constant profanity, smoking and drinking, and a knifepoint theft that goes unpunished; no hope beyond this life is offered.

frames_add.aligns: Comfort and meaning come from human bonds and a stranger's kindness, and the story's answer to grief is to keep living.
frames_add.concerns: The stated childhood sexual abuse (likely ch. 1-3) and the handling of suicide against safe-messaging guidance.

frames_add.aligns: The story refuses easy answers about why Mariko died and leaves her last letter unread to the reader, an honest open ending.
frames_add.concerns: The stated childhood sexual abuse (likely ch. 1-3), a near-suicide (likely ch. 4) and self-harm.

frames_add.aligns: Fierce loyalty to a friend, a sense that the dead are still owed care, and a stranger who says the way to keep the dead is to go on living.
frames_add.concerns: The father is never held to account, and the stated abuse (likely ch. 1-3), suicide and near-suicide are heavy for younger teens.

frames_add.aligns: A wrongly accused father is cleared and the real killer is judged; revenge is finally given up for lawful justice (Romans 12:19); confession and remorse at the trial.
frames_add.concerns: Graphic torture-murders, nudity, sex scenes and a prostitution ring (rated 18+) fail the Philippians 4:8 test for most families; a dark mood with no spiritual hope.

frames_add.aligns: The case is solved by evidence and reason; identity is shown as chosen, not inherited from a father; no supernatural framing.
frames_add.concerns: Dissociative identity used mainly for plot twists; graphic cruelty to women as plot material.

frames_add.aligns: Honest about how little anyone knows of another person, or even of oneself; truth sought patiently; no preaching.
frames_add.concerns: Mental illness portrayed as dangerous and sensational; very graphic violence.

frames_add.aligns: Fairness wins: the innocent are cleared, the guilty face consequences, and a loyal friend waits at the end.
frames_add.concerns: An adult-only book: torture, sex scenes and nudity are well beyond a child's age; a heavy, bleak tone.

frames_add.aligns: A mocked boy finds his worth through honest craft, honors the grandfather who raised him (Ephesians 6:2), and the chaste romance ends in marriage and a child (ch. 107, 115).
frames_add.concerns: Constant fan-service framing of the bodies of 15- and 16-year-old characters (from ch. 2-3 on), a teen's love of adult games affirmed, a love-hotel photo shoot played as comedy (ch. 36), and a nun's habit used as costume.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning comes from craft, friendship and love, and the story rejects shaming people for their hobbies.
frames_add.concerns: The art sexualizes high-school-age characters, and a teen's restrictive diet goes unchallenged (likely ch. 56-60).

frames_add.aligns: Openness to many kinds of people and passions, with no worldview pressed on the reader.
frames_add.concerns: The same fan-service and diet-culture concerns critics raise.

frames_add.aligns: Loving what you love without shame, loyalty to friends, and a grandparent's craft carried on.
frames_add.concerns: Rated Mature in print and 15+ by Common Sense Media for frequent partial nudity and innuendo centered on minors; the diet pressure on a teen model.

frames_add.aligns: Abused children are rescued (Eri, vols. 14-18), a corrupt state commission is exposed (ch. 309-314), and second chances are real for a bully and an abusive father (ch. 323), close to Luke 4:18 and Matthew 5:44.
frames_add.concerns: Mineta's harassment is played for laughs, spirit-like vestiges live inside the hero's power, and trans-coded characters are a concern for many but not all families.

frames_add.aligns: Heroism comes from training, choice and human solidarity, and the epilogue gives power back to ordinary people who pool their skills for Deku (ch. 430-431).
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: harassment gags and heavy war violence in later volumes.

frames_add.aligns: Villains' grievances against hero society get a real hearing (Shigaraki, Stain, Lady Nagant), and the story preaches no faith or unbelief.
frames_add.concerns: Harassment gags and the abuse backstories (ch. 39, 236) need a conversation for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Friends who bring Deku home (ch. 319-323), everyday decency, second chances and a hero who helps without being asked fit this tradition closely.
frames_add.concerns: Later volumes bring war, mass casualties and dark abuse backstories, and early volumes have harassment gags.

frames_add.aligns: Honest about suffering and depression, it shows that purchased intimacy cannot fill the need for real love and worth, and recovery comes through perseverance and truth-telling.
frames_add.concerns: A paid sexual encounter between two women with nudity (ch. 1, 4) is presented sympathetically, not as sin, and self-cutting and an eating disorder are shown with no faith or church in view.

frames_add.aligns: Recovery comes through self-knowledge, honest work and human connection without supernatural rescue, and mental illness is described without shame.
frames_add.concerns: Self-harm with visible scars and an eating disorder are hard reading, and the adult nudity in the love-hotel scenes (ch. 1, 4) is not for younger teens.

frames_add.aligns: An honest, humble memoir that tests its own belief (that sex would fix loneliness) and finds it wanting, without preaching.
frames_add.concerns: Depression, self-cutting and adult nudity (ch. 1, 4) make it a book for older readers.

frames_add.aligns: Small, practical steps toward caring for oneself, and the lesson that inner peace can mean disappointing others' expectations.
frames_add.concerns: The sex-work premise and adult nudity (ch. 1, 4) will divide families, and the self-harm and eating-disorder content is beyond many teens.

frames_add.aligns: Education and hard work honored (Shizuku becomes a lawyer, Haru takes a research path); brothers reconcile; loyal friends; the story ends in marriage.
frames_add.concerns: The opening grab, threat and kiss without consent (ch. 1-2) are treated lightly; frequent fighting; teen dating as the premise.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning found in study, science and human connection; no supernatural claims; a family built by choice.
frames_add.concerns: Early aggression and a non-consensual kiss played as charm; possessiveness.

frames_add.aligns: Two guarded people learn to let others in; a family's coldness shown honestly; no preaching.
frames_add.concerns: The coercive opening scenes are never really addressed, critics say.

frames_add.aligns: Friendship, family repair, loyalty and a happy ending; finding your own path against family pressure.
frames_add.concerns: The forced kiss and the threat in the opening chapters; violence often solves problems.

frames_add.aligns: The costs of sexual sin and drugs are shown plainly (Galatians 6:7): a pregnancy, broken trust and Ren's death (ch. 77); Hachi keeps her child; friends care for the grieving (ch. 81-84); and the label boss and tabloids who exploit people are condemned.
frames_add.concerns: Sex outside marriage, heavy drinking and smoking are everyday, Ren's heroin use is supplied by his label boss (v11, v19), a 15-year-old band member is in a sexual relationship with an adult singer (v3-15), Hachi had an affair with a married man (v1), and no hope beyond human ties is offered.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is built through loyal human bonds and music, and grief, addiction and their consequences are shown honestly without supernatural framing.
frames_add.concerns: A 15-year-old in a sexual relationship with an adult (v3-15), Takumi's controlling treatment of Hachi not yet judged by the story, and drug and drinking culture styled as cool.

frames_add.aligns: The story refuses easy answers about love and happiness and, unfinished, leaves readers to draw their own conclusions.
frames_add.concerns: Exploitation of a minor, a coercive marriage and an atmosphere of heavy drinking, smoking and drug use.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friendship as the truest love, honesty (Junko), forgiveness and care for a grieving friend (ch. 81-84).
frames_add.concerns: Sex, alcohol and heroin throughout, an adult's relationship with a 15-year-old (v3-15), and flash-forwards in which the friendship is broken and Nana is missing.

frames_add.aligns: A rejected orphan is lifted up and earns trust, and he breaks the cycle of hatred by refusing revenge on the man who destroyed his village (ch. 443-453; Romans 12:19); elders and teachers pass on wisdom.
frames_add.concerns: Spirit summoning, reanimated dead and a blood-ritual cult (vol. 35-37) that Holiness families may treat as spiritually real; a peeping mentor shown as wise and drinking played for laughs; Common Sense Media says Killer Bee draws on stereotypes of Black people, though a Black fan writer also praises him.

frames_add.aligns: Peace comes from people understanding each other, with no god stepping in, and the only explicit religion belongs to a villain's fictional god.
frames_add.concerns: The late reincarnation-and-destiny reveal (ch. 671) cuts against 'hard work beats talent'.

frames_add.aligns: Shinto and Buddhist ideas appear as wonder and myth without any doctrine being pressed, and rival theories of peace each get a voice.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the violence.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends and village, never giving up, and parents who watch over and return to help their son (ch. 500-503).
frames_add.concerns: Constant battle violence, comic nudity gags and drinking (Common Sense Media: 11+, darker in Part II).

frames_add.aligns: The human plan to make humanity god-like collapses like Babel (Genesis 11), adults who use children are condemned, and Shinji chooses life with others (stages 91-95).
frames_add.concerns: Angels made into monsters and biblical names used as decoration with no God or gospel; nudity of 14-year-old characters (stages 14, 36); graphic deaths including a child's (stages 39-40); suicides.

frames_add.aligns: Human error causes the catastrophe and a human choice undoes it; the religious symbols are imagery with no acting God, and meaning comes from relationships (stages 71, 93-95).
frames_add.concerns: Nudity of 14-year-old characters (stages 14, 36), graphic violence including a 14-year-old's death (stages 39-40), and suicides that need mental-health framing.

frames_add.aligns: Big questions about self, others and what lies beyond are raised and left partly open, and the charismatic plotters who demand obedience (Seele, Gendo) fail.
frames_add.concerns: Nudity of minors (stages 14, 36), graphic violence (stages 39-40, 55, 85-88) and a heavy, despairing middle stretch before the hopeful end.

frames_add.aligns: A son's farewell to his mother's spirit and a restored world with new friendships (stages 95, Final) give a hopeful, spiritual-but-open ending; controlling institutions are exposed.
frames_add.concerns: Long stretches of despair and death, nudity of minors (stages 14, 36) and graphic violence make it heavy for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Kindness, peacemaking between rival families, friends who free Marika from a forced wedding (ch. 189-191), and one faithful marriage at the end (ch. 229).
frames_add.concerns: The premise is years of lying to parents (Proverbs 12:22), gangsters and guns are played as lovable comedy, and the hot-spring and beach chapters (ch. 22-23, 44) show fan service of high-school characters.

frames_add.aligns: Love is built by honest choice rather than fate: Raku sets aside a childhood promise to choose the person he grew to love (ch. 227).
frames_add.concerns: Slapstick violence by a girl toward a boy is a running joke, organized crime is shown as harmless, and there is light fan service (ch. 22-23).

frames_add.aligns: Destiny and choice are weighed fairly, Kosaki's destined love is honored even as Raku chooses otherwise, and no belief is pushed.
frames_add.concerns: Light fan service, guns as gags and the comic glamour of yakuza families.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, everyday kindness and a happy future for every character reward decency; a temple festival (ch. 42) is ordinary background.
frames_add.concerns: A long deception of parents, hitting as a joke, and some bath and beach fan service.

frames_add.aligns: Wrongdoing harms those bound to us and is healed by confession and cleansing (Yukine's blight and ablution, v3; 1 John 1:9), a boy abused to death and a god made into a killer are shown as wronged, and a being can turn from a violent past.
frames_add.concerns: The heroes are gods of other religions shown as real and good, spirits of the dead are bound to serve them, and the story journeys to an underworld (ch. 30-35), which Holiness and Pentecostal families may see as spiritually real (Deuteronomy 18:10-12); light fan service and suicide themes appear.

frames_add.aligns: A made being rejects the purpose his maker gave him and chooses his own, and harsh divine courts are questioned (ch. 70-72).
frames_add.concerns: The resolution rests on a believer's faithful remembrance keeping a god alive (ch. 109), and suicide themes need care.

frames_add.aligns: Gods are shown as flawed, comic and dependent on human memory, sacred things are handled with both humor and affection, and no single doctrine is pressed on the reader.
frames_add.concerns: Spirits of the dead serving gods and the suicide-adjacent scenes (likely ch. 4) call for discussion.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, second chances, ties that outlast forgetting (ch. 108-109), and a spirit world where good and bad deeds have consequences.
frames_add.concerns: Sword violence, Yukine's abuse backstory and a few suicide-adjacent scenes.

frames_add.aligns: Freeing the enslaved is the story's core (ch. 502, 521; Fish-Man Island, vols. 62-66), racism is condemned, and revenge is rejected even for real wrongs, echoing the Exodus and Luke 4:18.
frames_add.concerns: Heroes drink and smoke freely, fan service and harassment gags recur (vols. 46-48, 53), Luffy is given a sun-god identity (ch. 1044), and gender-variant characters are a concern for many but not all families.

frames_add.aligns: Self-proclaimed gods are exposed as tyrants (Enel; the Celestial Dragons), scholars and books are defended against a state that burns them (Ohara, vol. 41), and meaning lives on through human inherited will.
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: fan service and violence as the default way problems end.

frames_add.aligns: Myth and mystery (Nika, the Void Century, Elbaph's gods) are treated with wonder rather than doctrine, and no faith is pushed.
frames_add.concerns: Sexualized art and harassment gags recur across a very long series.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends who would die for you, fairness for the oppressed, and the dead living on through those who carry their will are the heart of the story.
frames_add.concerns: Fan service and constant fighting, plus a few very dark backstories (Kuma, vols. 108-109), call for an age check.

frames_add.aligns: Doing good unseen and without reward (Matthew 6:1-4), humility, and the courage of the weakest hero (Mumen Rider, ch. 26-28) are honored, and the being called God who buys loyalty with power is shown as a threat.
frames_add.concerns: Fan service presented for enjoyment, a gay character used partly as a joke (Puri-Puri Prisoner), and frequent gore.

frames_add.aligns: Strength comes from plain training, institutions and prophecy are treated with skepticism, and the only god is a manipulator; meaning comes from ordinary goods and helping people.
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: gore played for comedy and fan service, including a young-looking adult woman.

frames_add.aligns: Saitama's search for meaning after winning is explored honestly and left open, and the story preaches nothing.
frames_add.concerns: Saitama's emptiness is unresolved and may need a conversation; fan service recurs.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning in small everyday goods (groceries on sale, meals with friends), fairness to the outsider Garou, and decency without needing praise fit this tradition well.
frames_add.concerns: Frequent gore and fan service (Tatsumaki, Fubuki) call for an age check.

frames_add.aligns: Friends who refuse to give up on a hurting classmate bear one another's burdens (Galatians 6:2), and hope wins over despair when Kakeru chooses life (Last Letter, v5).
frames_add.concerns: A teen's suicide in one timeline and his mother's suicide (Letters 1-2, Letter 19) with no prayer, church or adult help shown; hope has no source beyond friendship.

frames_add.aligns: The letters are explained by science, not miracle, and Kakeru's worth and reason to live come entirely from the people around him (v1-v5).
frames_add.concerns: No doctor, counselor or adult helps on the page, so the rescue rests on teenagers; suicide content needs safe-messaging care (Letter 19, v5).

frames_add.aligns: Takes no side on faith; ethics rest on empathy and honesty, and the bittersweet ending leaves the old timeline's loss standing without false comfort (v5).
frames_add.concerns: Suicide is central (Letters 1-2, 19) and no professional help appears until vol. 7's lesson that asking for help is not weakness.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, everyday decency and a second chance carry the story; a New Year's shrine visit sits lightly as custom (v4).
frames_add.concerns: The weight of a teen's suicide and a parent's suicide (Letters 1-2, 19) may be too much for younger or vulnerable readers.

frames_add.aligns: The exploitation of young performers, stalking and the online pile-on that nearly kills Akane (v3) are all framed as wrong, and Ai's last message wishes her betrayer could learn to love.
frames_add.concerns: Aqua's revenge ends in a murder-suicide presented as loving sacrifice (ch. 162-164), against Romans 12:19; reincarnation as premise; the twins' past-life romance (ch. 123, 143); frequent profanity.

frames_add.aligns: A sharp look at how media editing and fandom manipulate people, with rebirth used only as a story device.
frames_add.concerns: Private revenge over evidence and courts, ending in a murder-suicide framed as noble.

frames_add.aligns: The rebirth and the mysterious child at Takachiho (v8) are left unexplained, a mystery rather than a doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: The ending presents self-destruction as peace, which many readers found troubling.

frames_add.aligns: A mother's love that outlasts death and siblings who protect each other; fame and online cruelty are exposed.
frames_add.concerns: A suicide attempt (v3), the abuse of a minor in the villain's backstory and a despairing ending put it at 15+ (Common Sense Media).

frames_add.aligns: A teen at the edge of suicide is pulled back by a welcoming community (ch. 1-5), slurs and contempt are shown as wrong, and those who wounded others apologize and are restored (Tsubaki, vol. 3; Misora, vol. 4).
frames_add.concerns: A same-sex wedding as the happy ending and gender transition affirmed, which differ from the official teaching of most of these churches though members' views vary; suicide content; a child is groped at a festival, condemned by the story (ch. 9).

frames_add.aligns: Rescue and dignity come from human community and empathy with no supernatural help, and prejudice is shown giving way to understanding (vol. 3-4).
frames_add.concerns: Suicide content (ch. 1) needs care for younger readers, and Someone-san's 'jumps' are left as unexplained magical realism.

frames_add.aligns: Refuses easy labels and final answers about the self, holding that one need not fully understand oneself to be respected (ch. 21; Kamatani).
frames_add.concerns: A teen's near-suicide (ch. 1), frequent slurs and a child groped at a festival (ch. 9), all shown as harmful.

frames_add.aligns: Finding your own path among people who accept you, everyday decency, and a farewell at a partner's deathbed (vol. 4) match these families' values.
frames_add.concerns: Heavy themes (suicide, outing, slurs, ch. 1, 9, vol. 4) for younger readers; families vary on the same-sex wedding.

frames_add.aligns: A boy told his very existence is a sin learns his worth, a fraudulent cult that preys on orphans is exposed (ch. 52-57), and forgiveness changes Vincent (ch. 97), in the spirit of Psalm 139:14.
frames_add.concerns: Power comes from contracts sealed by drinking monsters' blood and from soul transfer, the ending is reincarnation (ch. 104), and Alice's suicide is framed as sacrifice (ch. 78).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is made by people who choose to go on; a cult selling paradise is exposed as a fraud, and the heroes refuse a comforting dream of an undone past (ch. 104).
frames_add.concerns: Alice's suicide (ch. 78) and Vincent's wish to erase himself need mental-health framing; beheadings in the cult arc (ch. 54-57).

frames_add.aligns: Questions of identity, memory and what lies beyond are left open with wonder, and the rebirth epilogue (ch. 104) is offered as a gift, not a doctrine.
frames_add.concerns: A suicide framed as sacrifice (ch. 78) and heavy gore in the middle arcs.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty among friends, a promise kept across a century, and the reunion of Oz, Alice and Gilbert in a new life (ch. 104) reward hope.
frames_add.concerns: Most of the cast dies in the final arc, and a suicide and beheadings (ch. 54-57, 78) make it a dark read.

frames_add.aligns: Evil is shown as evil, a mother's sacrificial love is honored (ch. 9, 48), an elder's care restores the hero (ch. 59-60), and mercy is held up as what makes us human (ch. 62).
frames_add.concerns: Two high-school students have sex (ch. 57) and crude sexual gags involve the teen lead (ch. 2); extreme gore; a view of humans as one animal among many without the image of God (Genesis 1:27).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is made without God, and reason, science and empathy together define humanity (ch. 25, 62-63).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving 17-year-olds (ch. 2, 57) and heavy gore.

frames_add.aligns: The big question of what makes us human is wrestled with honestly, and Reiko dies having found only more questions (ch. 48).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving 17-year-olds (ch. 2, 57); body horror for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Love for family and friends, an old woman's kindness to a stranger (ch. 59-60), and a serial killer who claims murder is human nature firmly rejected (ch. 64).
frames_add.concerns: Graphic violence, the deaths of the hero's mother and friends, and sexual content involving teens (ch. 2, 57).

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, care in sickness, and parents who are present in their children's lives (ch. 81-83, 100-114).
frames_add.concerns: A high-school girl's unsupervised overnight stays in a boy's apartment are treated as charming and blessed by parents, with regular fan service of a 16-17-year-old, an adult-video scene (vol. 1) and an accidental-nudity gag (vol. 3); truancy and dropping college plans for a girlfriend (vols. 9-10).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is found in ordinary companionship, with no villains and no cruelty.
frames_add.concerns: Teasing about the body and the adult-video scene (vol. 1) raise boundary and consent questions, and the heroine is a minor drawn for fan service.

frames_add.aligns: A gentle, unpreachy story of two awkward people learning to be honest with each other (vol. 8).
frames_add.concerns: Fan service of a 16-17-year-old (vols. 1-3) for an older-reader imprint; age-appropriateness for teen readers.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, friends who look out for each other and families who end up approving the couple.
frames_add.concerns: Raunchy fan service with high-school characters (vols. 1-3) and teens left alone overnight with no adult present.

frames_add.aligns: Forgiveness over revenge (Romans 12:19); an anti-robot hate group modeled on the Klan is condemned; love for the despised and care for orphans.
frames_add.concerns: Whether a made being has a soul; death-god names; a war allegory some families will read differently.

frames_add.aligns: Personhood judged by mind and feeling, not origin; reason and empathy against prejudice and a war built on lies.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; some will discuss whether the story makes AI too human.

frames_add.aligns: Leaves open whether a made mind has a heart or soul; humility about what minds are; ethics grounded in empathy.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise.

frames_add.aligns: Decency, grief honored and loyalty to family and friends; hatred laid down at the end.
frames_add.concerns: Violence and many deaths among characters readers come to love.

frames_add.aligns: Friends who stand by each other under unjust, humiliating authority, and a betrayer (Shingo) who is restored, fit the call to loyalty and forgiveness.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving minors runs through the series (a 15-year-old in nude and fetish scenes, ch. 39, 120, 177-178, 207-208), degradation is the joke, and the peeping premise clashes with Matthew 5:28 and the Philippians 4:8 test.

frames_add.aligns: Planning, reason and loyalty beat arbitrary, blackmailing authority on both student councils (vols. 4-9, 18-25).
frames_add.concerns: The comedy depends on sexualizing and degrading teen characters, including a 15-year-old (ch. 39, 120, 177-178), which runs against consent and harm-based ethics.

frames_add.aligns: Mocks anyone who claims total control over others and rewards friends who keep faith with each other.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving minors and humiliation as humor (ch. 39, 89, 120, 177-178); the publisher rates it 18+.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends, payback for wrongdoing (the boys are jailed for peeping) and distrust of controlling institutions all land with these families.
frames_add.concerns: Rated 18+ by its publisher: pervasive sexual content with high-school characters (ch. 39, 120, 177-178, 207-208) and crude degradation played for laughs.

frames_add.aligns: The worth of every person whatever their body (1 Corinthians 12:22), perseverance through suffering (Romans 5:3-4), and Nomiya's guilt turning into responsibility and amends.
frames_add.concerns: Profanity, street fights and Nomiya's jail stay (v15), and Takahashi's self-harm and despair (v2-3); hope rests on human effort alone.

frames_add.aligns: Recovery comes from medicine, rehab, practice and friends, with no supernatural rescue, and meaning is rebuilt in this life.
frames_add.concerns: The self-harm scene (v2-3) needs care; one critic reads Takahashi's crash after a theft as karmic punishment.

frames_add.aligns: Honest about suffering without offering a doctrine either way; humility replaces Takahashi's ranking of people.
frames_add.concerns: Despair and the self-harm scene (v2-3) are heavy; little else to raise.

frames_add.aligns: Everyday decency, loyalty between friends, a father and son reconciled (v12) and consequences that feel fair.
frames_add.concerns: Swearing, fights and the self-harm scene (v2-3).

frames_add.aligns: Adam fights Zeus to protect his descendants without hatred (Round 2, ch. 7-12), and humanity stands up to an arrogant power that has condemned it.
frames_add.concerns: Jesus appears as a silent 'sage' among philosophers at a death match (ch. 46), against John 14:6; Eden is retold so that the Fall is the gods' injustice rather than human sin (Genesis 3); many gods are shown as real, Satan and demons are given sympathetic backstories (Round 8), and goddess fan service recurs.

frames_add.aligns: Gods are arrogant judges whom humans beat by their own skill and courage, and Tesla's science matches divine power (Round 8); religious figures are treated as story material.
frames_add.concerns: Human worth is proved by winning fights to the death, and a serial killer (Jack the Ripper, Round 4) is cast as humanity's champion.

frames_add.aligns: Many traditions' gods and founders appear side by side with no single faith declared true, and the reader is left to weigh whether the gods have any right to judge humanity.
frames_add.concerns: Sacred figures of living faiths (Shiva, the Buddha, Jesus) are used as tournament characters, which members of those faiths have objected to (Hindu objection, 2020-21).

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to family and to all of humanity, protective fathers (Adam), and respect earned even from enemies.
frames_add.concerns: Constant graphic violence in which defeated fighters' souls are destroyed outright, with little hope offered beyond winning.

frames_add.aligns: Workplace cruelty and sexism are condemned, the shut-in and the jobless are treated with dignity, and a man who has given up is given a second chance and learns to love his neighbor (Luke 10).
frames_add.concerns: Renewal comes through a company program with no faith or prayer, a suicide backstory (likely ch. 89-92), adult smoking and drinking, and memories erased without consent.

frames_add.aligns: Renewal comes through honesty, friendship, effort and science, with meaning found in this life after failure.
frames_add.concerns: A company erases people's memories without consent and the story mostly accepts it (ch. 116, 155, 216).

frames_add.aligns: Despair is answered with humility and connection rather than doctrine, and the memory-erasure question is left for readers to weigh.
frames_add.concerns: The suicide backstory needs care, and the consent problem in the experiment is softened by a happy ending.

frames_add.aligns: Second chances, loyalty among friends, a grave visit to honor the dead (ch. 92) and a hopeful reunion (ch. 221) reward everyday decency.
frames_add.concerns: A colleague's suicide after harassment is the core backstory, and adult smoking and drinking are played lightly.

frames_add.aligns: A young man gives months of hard work to make a film so a dying grandmother can see her granddaughter act (ch. 102-167), elders are loved, and a grieving young woman learns to accept help.
frames_add.concerns: A lie to sick grandparents and parents is kept up for hundreds of chapters (from ch. 1; Proverbs 12:22), the hero's lust and masturbation are running jokes with an explicit fantasy in ch. 218, fan service is frequent, and companionship is sold by the hour.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is found in human relationships and creative work, and loneliness is treated with candor rather than shame.
frames_add.concerns: The long deception of family is partly excused (ch. 150), and critics question whether the story critiques or rewards the hero's entitlement.

frames_add.aligns: The story leaves open whether bought intimacy can become real and lets readers weigh Chizuru's right to say 'not now' (ch. 380).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual humor and fan service, and a lie that drags on far longer than its consequences.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to grandparents, perseverance and sincere effort for someone you love.
frames_add.concerns: Years of lying to family, frequent sexual comedy and fan service (rated 16+ in print), and a paid-companionship premise.

frames_add.aligns: Welcome for someone who is different, honesty in conflict, a mother's steady love and a class that chooses to keep its outsider (ch. 39-40), in the spirit of treating every person with dignity.
frames_add.concerns: Some families associate dragons with Satan (Revelation 12:9), though here they are animals studied by science; the absent father and the mother's admission about raising Ruri alone (ch. 46).

frames_add.aligns: Dragon traits are studied with blood tests and explained as biology (ch. 20, 48), and problems are solved by honest talk.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; the state bureau monitoring a teenager goes largely unquestioned (ch. 22, 32).

frames_add.aligns: Curiosity rather than fear meets the unknown, and classmates who misjudged Ruri are allowed to learn and change (ch. 13-15, 24).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends, a caring mother and everyday decency; Kashiro waits at the finish line after Ruri pushes her away (ch. 29-31).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond Ruri's brief despair (ch. 37-38), which friends help her through.

frames_add.aligns: A former killer is changed by love, becomes a faithful husband and father, makes amends by helping others, shows mercy to his defeated enemy and leaves judgment to lawful authority (ch. 282-283; Romans 12:19, 13:4).
frames_add.concerns: Constant stylized gunfights and blood, frequent profanity in the anime, weight jokes about the hero, and allies who still kill shown as cool.

frames_add.aligns: Life is valued without religious grounding, people can change, and courts rather than vengeance decide the villain's fate.
frames_add.concerns: Glamorized assassin culture for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: A humane, preach-free story of second chances that leaves families to draw their own conclusions.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the violence.

frames_add.aligns: Family first, loyal friends, everyday decency and the idea that it is never too late to start over.
frames_add.concerns: Gore, swearing and weight jokes (Common Sense Media: 16+ for the anime; ScreenWise: 14+ for the manga).

frames_add.aligns: Orphans farmed for blood and children used as weapons are framed as evil, and Yu keeps faith with his chosen family; deliverance from bondage echoes the Exodus.
frames_add.concerns: Heroes draw power from demon pacts, angels are recast as weapons and God appears mainly as a punisher; suggestive blood-feeding involving young characters (ch. 1, Krul and Mika) and constant violence.

frames_add.aligns: Human loyalty outweighs every divine or institutional scheme, cults are exposed, and accepting death is treated as wise.
frames_add.concerns: The prostitution parallel in ch. 1 and sexually coded feeding of a teen by a child-looking vampire; suicide pills (Code 284); heavy gore.

frames_add.aligns: The cosmic myth of angels and a punishing God stays fiction, and the story leaves big questions about death and grief open while the ending is pending.
frames_add.concerns: Biblical names used freely in an invented theology may confuse readers; the same depiction concerns about young characters.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to chosen family over every plan; institutions that control children (the Hiragi clan, cults, the vampire council) are shown as the danger.
frames_add.concerns: Grief that refuses to let the dead go ends the world; dark, violent and often hopeless in tone.

frames_add.aligns: A faithful, honest couple, warm parents and a strong young woman who protects others; a rival treated with grace (vol. 12).
frames_add.concerns: Teen dating as the story's center, an unchaperoned overnight trip at 18 (ch. 175-176) and an epilogue plan to live together before marriage.

frames_add.aligns: A healthy relationship built on communication and mutual support, with no supernatural framing.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise.

frames_add.aligns: Gentle and humane; temple visits shown as ordinary life without any claim.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, everyday kindness and supportive families and friends.
frames_add.concerns: Mild fan service; the overnight trip and cohabitation plan may be a family conversation.

frames_add.aligns: Education pursued in order to serve one's community, a hardworking family that is honored, kindness across social lines, and an abusive mother who repents and seeks help (ch. 67, 71).
frames_add.concerns: The affirming portrayal of Mitsumi's aunt Nao as a transgender woman (ch. 2, 29, 55) differs from the official teaching of most of these churches, which many families will want to discuss; the childhood drinking scandal in Shima's past (ch. 23, 46).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is built from honest relationships, study and chosen work, and people grow by dropping their masks, with no supernatural framing.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise.

frames_add.aligns: People of very different backgrounds are shown fairly, and characters who misjudged others are allowed to learn (ch. 5, 14-15).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; the big questions are left aside rather than explored.

frames_add.aligns: Family love, loyal friends, everyday decency and a hometown worth serving (ch. 51-56).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond Shima's memories of his mother's abuse (ch. 46).

frames_add.aligns: A former gang leader weeps, asks to come back and is received by a forgiving elder (v8; Luke 15), a delinquent is remade by humble practice, and perseverance through loss is honored (v15, v30).
frames_add.concerns: Fistfights and headbutts are played for laughs early (v1-2), swearing is frequent in English versions, and the 'Gorilla' nickname rests on 1990s colorism, which these families are likely to notice.

frames_add.aligns: Human effort, practice and teamwork transform people with no supernatural help, and failure becomes a lesson.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond comic violence early and honoring play through injury (v30).

frames_add.aligns: Rival teams and approaches are treated with respect, and no side is preached at.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; religion appears only as a nickname and a prayer to a coach's photo.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to the team, second chances, fair play rewarded and dirty play beaten (v23-24), and a coach who never gives up on his players.
frames_add.concerns: Early comic fighting, swearing and name-calling (v1-8).

frames_add.aligns: A man stands up for a frightened young worker against an abusive customer (Smoke 0), overworked people are treated with dignity, and the romance stays chaste and respectful.
frames_add.concerns: Tobacco is the bond and comfort at the heart of the story, and the one health warning is reversed so Sasaki resumes smoking (vol. 1); private night meetings, a hidden identity, and a 21-year age gap.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is found in human connection, small daily goods and kindness, with no supernatural framing.
frames_add.concerns: The X-ray chapter turns medical evidence about smoking into a punchline (vol. 1), and the habit is framed as harmless comfort.

frames_add.aligns: A gentle, humble story about tired adults that pushes no worldview and values empathy and honesty.
frames_add.concerns: Smoking is glamorized, and Yamada's hidden identity is a deception the story only gently questions.

frames_add.aligns: Everyday decency, kindness to a stranger repaid years later, and co-workers who look after each other.
frames_add.concerns: Smoking is shown as the path to friendship and love, with a reversed health scare (vol. 1); the age gap is worth discussing.

frames_add.aligns: Courage, perseverance and hard work; mercy to the baby Sophia; a church that uses religion for war is condemned.
frames_add.concerns: Reincarnation and gods shown as powers rather than good; magic and evil gods; pride ranked above humility; gore and cannibalism.

frames_add.aligns: Reason, experiment and evidence: Kumoko tests skills and theories; gods are not good just because they are powerful.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty played for laughs; thousands killed lightly.

frames_add.aligns: Gods are shown as flawed managers and no faith is pushed; the world's rules are investigated rather than assumed.
frames_add.concerns: Mass killing and gore treated lightly.

frames_add.aligns: Grit, finding your own path, and a loner who slowly gains a family.
frames_add.concerns: Violence and cannibalism played for comedy; little sense of fairness for the many killed.

frames_add.aligns: Honest work, loyal friends and a mother's quiet care carry Meiko through grief, and she endures and goes on (2 Corinthians 4:8-9).
frames_add.concerns: An unmarried couple lives together as a matter of course, grief is met with no prayer or hope of resurrection, and swearing and drinking are likely (to verify).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is found in work, art, love and friendship, and grief is faced honestly without supernatural comfort, carried forward through the dead man's song (ch. 26-28).
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; the possible reading of Taneda's crash as deliberate (around ch. 14) needs mental-health care.

frames_add.aligns: The story refuses a neat answer about dreams versus stability and makes no claim about what lies beyond death.
frames_add.concerns: The ambiguous framing of Taneda's death deserves a careful talk.

frames_add.aligns: Friends who hold each other up, a loving mother, and a widow who carries her partner's song into an ordinary, hopeful life (ch. 29).
frames_add.concerns: A sudden death and long grief; some readers read the crash as possibly intentional.

frames_add.aligns: Courage overcomes fear (2 Timothy 1:7), an abused child is shown mercy and redeemed (ch. 112), and a long persecution ends in a truce (ch. 113).
frames_add.concerns: A friendly death god, real witches and souls harvested and eaten are the fabric of the world, which Holiness and Pentecostal families read against Deuteronomy 18:10-12; nudity, peeping and groping of girls played as jokes (prologues 1-3, ch. 73-75); Crona's self-harm (ch. 17).

frames_add.aligns: The era of the gods ends and people build their own world (ch. 113), and blind faith in a god alone is shown as a danger (Justin, ch. 86).
frames_add.concerns: Fan service that objectifies girls, including teenagers, is played as humor, and the series treats madness as a spiritual force rather than an illness.

frames_add.aligns: Asura's charge that Death defines 'normal' by whim gets a hearing, and neither absolute order nor madness is declared the answer.
frames_add.concerns: Objectifying fan service and crude jokes, heaviest in the first volumes, and a violent fantasy setting.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal partners, courage against fear, souls and fate taken half-seriously, and old enemies reconciled at the end (ch. 113).
frames_add.concerns: Fan service and sexual jokes involving teenage girls, gore, and a child's abuse and self-harm (ch. 17-19) are beyond younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Adopting and protecting an orphan (James 1:27), a home that grows into real love, peace-making, and a teacher who speaks truth against war propaganda at real cost (Mission 99).
frames_add.concerns: The family is built on lies that are not yet judged (Proverbs 12:22), the mother's killing work is often played lightly (Mission 2), and drunkenness is used as comedy (Missions 79-80).

frames_add.aligns: Human care and reason solve problems with no faith content at all, the schoolhouse ghost turns out to be a person (Mission 124), and war is shown as human suffering.
frames_add.concerns: Graded on harm: comic violence and harsh interrogations played lightly.

frames_add.aligns: No belief is pushed, both sides of the cold war get sympathetic characters, and the big questions about honesty and love are left open while the series continues.
frames_add.concerns: Lying and killing as a job are rarely examined and may need a conversation.

frames_add.aligns: A loving family built by choice, loyalty, everyday kindness and protecting children are the heart of the story.
frames_add.concerns: Comic violence, a mother who is a paid assassin, and drunkenness played for laughs.

frames_add.aligns: Rape, trafficking and the abuse of the young are condemned, Ken says a victim is not defiled, and the ending turns from revenge (Romans 12:19).
frames_add.concerns: A gang boss who runs casinos and sex businesses is the admired hero; constant gang violence and sexual violence; sources report sexual content involving under-18 characters in backstories (details unconfirmed).

frames_add.aligns: Human dignity apart from what is done to the body, and an ending that chooses reason over revenge.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual violence used again and again as drama, reported sexual content involving under-18 characters, and cruelty as spectacle.

frames_add.aligns: No preaching; the turn away from revenge after a victim's family's letter is offered as a hard-won choice.
frames_add.concerns: The same concerns about sexual violence, exploitation of women and reported scenes involving minors.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to friends and protecting the poor (the food-stall owner) drive the hero.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty and crime are admired in the hero's world; sexual violence and reported scenes involving under-18 characters.

frames_add.aligns: Shows sin and harm passing from adults to children; confession and turning oneself in (Naoki); a self-giving sacrifice that opens a new start (ch. 15-16); friendship that refuses to give up.
frames_add.concerns: A 9-year-old's suicide shown in ch. 1 and a teen's suicide later; long stretches of despair; a child killed and hidden by children; no God answers.

frames_add.aligns: No magic fix and no god rescues anyone; help comes from listening, honesty and friendship (ch. 10, 16); problems have many human causes.
frames_add.concerns: The suicide method is shown (ch. 1); a hard read for children who are bullied or have suicidal thoughts.

frames_add.aligns: Refuses easy answers and assigns no single villain; Shizuka's loss of faith is shown without mockery or reward.
frames_add.concerns: Child suicide and killing shown directly; some critics find the ending too neat for children who need real help.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, forgiveness and friendship win in the end (ch. 16); being heard by one person changes a life (ch. 10).
frames_add.concerns: Despair and child suicide are shown plainly; VIZ rates it Mature and School Library Journal suggests grade 10 and up.

frames_add.aligns: Clean humor, kindness, honesty and patience; a confession at the end (v20) and flash-forwards to a happy marriage.
frames_add.concerns: Puberty jokes and swimsuit chapters with 13- and 14-year-olds; early-teen crushes; shrine fortunes kept as custom.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning in ordinary days and human kindness; no supernatural claims beyond custom.
frames_add.concerns: Whether constant teasing models good boundaries; little else.

frames_add.aligns: Gentle, unpreachy and warm; customs and legends shown lightly.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise.

frames_add.aligns: Everyday decency, loyalty and a sweet first love; seasonal festivals and shrine visits as family-style custom.
frames_add.concerns: A few puberty jokes and swimsuit chapters for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Outsiders and 'monsters' are welcomed as neighbors, former enemies such as the orcs are forgiven (likely v4-5), orphaned children are taught (v11), and the binding of summoned people like slaves is opposed.
frames_add.concerns: The hero answers an attack by killing an entire army to harvest souls (ch. 64-68), which the story treats as justified rather than leaving vengeance to God (Romans 12:19), and he becomes a Demon Lord who summons and names demons as servants and revives the dead (ch. 67-69); the only church is corrupt.

frames_add.aligns: Reason, education and practical problem-solving build a peaceful society of many kinds of people, and a corrupt church is exposed.
frames_add.concerns: Thousands of people are used as means to an end (ch. 64-68), and a single ruler with unlimited power is never held to account.

frames_add.aligns: Different peoples and beliefs learn to live side by side, and the hostile Holy Church is later reconciled with Tempest.
frames_add.concerns: Followers revere an all-powerful ruler with near-unquestioning devotion, and the story presents its hardest moral choice, the massacre, as settled rather than open.

frames_add.aligns: Friendship across differences, loyalty, hard work and a home where everyone belongs.
frames_add.concerns: The kind hero's slow killing of a fleeing army is rewarded with no consequence (ch. 64-66), and a demon created from the dead soldiers' bodies is the most popular character.

frames_add.aligns: Truth-telling and care for lonely or mistreated people, such as Shizuka and her mother's repentance (ch. 134-135), fit the call to lift up the lowly (Luke 1:52).
frames_add.concerns: One boy with dozens of partners sets aside marriage as one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24); sexual content involving minors is present (fan service with teen and junior-high characters, ch. 8, 14.5, 44, 69-70), adult staff are written as partners of a student (ch. 57, 213), and a forced-kissing gag recurs from ch. 2.

frames_add.aligns: The shrine god is a comic device and the characters' goodness comes from honesty and empathy toward each other (ch. 14-23).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving minors is present (teen and junior-high characters, ch. 8, 44, 69-70), adult staff partner a student (ch. 57, 213), and forced kissing is played for laughs, which clashes with consent and harm-based ethics.

frames_add.aligns: No faith or anti-faith message is pressed; the story's ethic of honest communication and not leaving anyone out rests on empathy (ch. 14-19, 146).
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving minors is present (ch. 8, 44, 69-70), adults in authority are partners of a student (ch. 57, 213), and the forced-kissing gag is never answered by the story.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, fairness and a chosen family where no one is left out (ch. 14, 146), with a light, fate-binding god that does not demand belief.
frames_add.concerns: Content well beyond a young reader's age: sexual content involving minors (ch. 8, 44, 69-70), adult staff as partners of a student (ch. 57, 213), forced kissing as a gag; the many-partner premise will divide families.

frames_add.aligns: A kidnapped, low-born young woman keeps her integrity in a corrupt court, as Esther did; healing serves the sick and poor, and a predatory late emperor is exposed (ch. 55-58).
frames_add.concerns: A brothel and concubinage are the normal setting and sex work is shown without moral judgment; frequent alcohol, tobacco, aphrodisiacs and the heroine's self-poisoning (ch. 2, 14, 24).

frames_add.aligns: Curses and ghosts are traced to lead, arsenic and human schemes (ch. 1, 56-59, 67), and careful testing saves lives.
frames_add.concerns: Maomao's habit of testing poisons on herself needs real-world framing for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Rites are shown with respect while superstition is corrected, so evidence is honored without sneering at belief.
frames_add.concerns: Every mystery gets a natural answer; the self-poisoning and drug content.

frames_add.aligns: Everyday decency, care for the people in front of you, a loving adoptive father, and wrongdoers who face fair consequences.
frames_add.concerns: Frequent drinking and drugs, a brothel setting, and ghosts that are almost always explained away.

frames_add.aligns: Children used as lab subjects are shown as a grave wrong, mercy and honest friendship gain ground over hatred, and the sincere believer Roland prays and weeps for others (Mémoire 47).
frames_add.concerns: The Church appears mainly as an armed persecutor teaching that some are beyond God's love; grimoires and curses; the hero's forced kiss framed romantically (Mémoire 4); a child's sexual exploitation is stated in vol. 9.

frames_add.aligns: Fanatical religious and aristocratic authority is exposed, human dignity is defended against experiments, and mortality is faced without supernatural comfort.
frames_add.concerns: The forced kiss is played partly as romance (Mémoire 4), blood-drinking without consent recurs, and child abuse in Moreau's lab is heavy (Mémoire 17-21, 48; vol. 9).

frames_add.aligns: No faction is innocent and fanaticism on both sides is shown destroying the people it claims to protect, while a sincere believer is drawn with sympathy.
frames_add.concerns: Consent problems in the romance and blood scenes (Mémoire 4, 27) and the stated sexual exploitation of a child (vol. 9).

frames_add.aligns: Chosen families repair broken ones (Mémoire 56), friendship survives a near-fatal fight, and controlling institutions are shown for what they are.
frames_add.concerns: Beheadings and lab horror involving children (Mémoire 8, 17-21) and the forced kiss (Mémoire 4) make it a series for older teens.

frames_add.aligns: Endurance through suffering, temptation resisted, and a lonely man brought home to a wife and child (ch. 129 to the final chapter).
frames_add.concerns: Long despair with no turn to God, needless risk to life (ch. 1, 13), a suicide attempt in the backstory and sexual scenes in the Yumi chapters (likely ch. 98-101).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is made in a finite life by effort and human bonds in an indifferent nature, with religion only as metaphor.
frames_add.concerns: Risk is given some glamour and depression goes untreated, so mental-health context helps.

frames_add.aligns: Why Mori climbs is left for the reader to weigh, and the story ends without forcing a single answer about meaning.
frames_add.concerns: Suicide-adjacent scenes (backstory; likely ch. 142) need care for vulnerable readers.

frames_add.aligns: Family and belonging win over solitary glory, and Mori comes home alive (final chapter).
frames_add.concerns: Long stretches of despair, deaths and frightening imagery, plus sexual chapters (likely ch. 98-101) that sit above the T+ rating.

frames_add.aligns: A boy's heart turns from contempt to love after he is loved first (1 John 4:19), and kindness, honesty and respect for boundaries win (vols. 2-14).
frames_add.concerns: Crude sexual talk and at times suggestive art of 13-to-15-year-old characters (v1-8; Ephesians 4:29), early-teen dating with a found-condom plot and time alone together (v10-13), and profanity.

frames_add.aligns: Growth comes from empathy, friendship and honest communication with no supernatural frame, and the edgy pose of contempt is outgrown (after v1).
frames_add.concerns: Sexualized jokes and suggestive drawings of middle school characters (v1-8) deserve a critical eye.

frames_add.aligns: A gentle story about seeing the good in others and choosing who to be, with no preaching either way.
frames_add.concerns: The murder-fantasy opening (v1) and puberty sexual humor involving 13-to-15-year-olds.

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends, a kind girl who sees the best in an outsider, and a boy who learns decency fit these families' values well.
frames_add.concerns: Crude talk and suggestive art involving middle schoolers (v1-8) and how far the early-teen couple goes in later volumes (v10-13) are age questions.

frames_add.aligns: A demon cult that experiments on the sick is exposed and defeated, outcast girls are healed (v1), and Cid protects his sister.
frames_add.concerns: The hero kills bandits for sport (v1, v7), lies as a way of life and is rewarded for self-glory; the only church is tied to the cult; fan service; a suicide attempt (v6).

frames_add.aligns: Planning and modern knowledge win (v9-10), and a compromised church and cult-like devotion are shown for what they are.
frames_add.concerns: Killing is played as fun with no accountability (v1, v7), and the hero shows little empathy.

frames_add.aligns: The story mocks grand certainty, since Cid's invented 'wisdom' is only borrowed knowledge (v13).
frames_add.concerns: A group that believes everything its leader says is shown as admirable and loyal; killing as comedy.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty among Shadow Garden, protecting family, and corrupt nobles and churchmen exposed.
frames_add.concerns: Cruelty played for laughs, a patricide and suicide attempt (v6), and fan service around devoted young women.

frames_add.aligns: Captives delivered (Misaki, ch. 55; Hinako, ch. 126-128); protecting the weak; honest work at a humble job; men who prey on women are punished.
frames_add.concerns: Justice done by gangsters and assassins rather than lawful authority (Romans 12:19, 13:1-4); sexual violence, nudity, drunkenness as comedy and profanity (rated 18+); a hero who killed 71 people is never asked to repent.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning found in ordinary work, comedy and friendship; problems solved by planning and reason; no supernatural frame.
frames_add.concerns: Justice outside the law; assassins made glamorous; sexual violence used for drama.

frames_add.aligns: A man learns to choose his own life; no preaching; both gangsters and ordinary people drawn with sympathy.
frames_add.concerns: Gangland violence and sexual violence shown often; the appeal of a cool killer.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty, gratitude and found family; the worst men get what is coming to them; a hopeful ending with a proposal.
frames_add.concerns: Adult content (18+): graphic violence, sexual violence and nudity are well beyond a child's age.

frames_add.aligns: Hidden sin grows and is found out (Numbers 32:23), and the second arc moves toward confession, facing those wronged and reconciliation (vol. 8-11).
frames_add.concerns: Nakamura's contempt and despair are voiced with sympathy and never answered by hope in God; the first arc involves 14-year-olds in theft of girls' clothing, a sexual assault of a boy by a girl (vol. 5) and a planned public self-immolation (vol. 6-7).

frames_add.aligns: A livable life is rebuilt in this world through honesty, friendship and creative work, and empty conformity is criticized without nihilism winning.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual content involving 14-year-olds, the little-addressed aftermath of a boy's assault (vol. 5) and the suicide plan (vol. 6-7) need care and context.

frames_add.aligns: Each teenager's view gets a sympathetic voice and consequences, not speeches, carry the verdicts, leaving the reader room to think.
frames_add.concerns: The anime stops before the recovery arc, and the festival suicide plan (vol. 6-7) and assault (vol. 5) are heavy for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: The story steps back from despair and ends with confession, forgiveness and ordinary lives that work (vol. 11).
frames_add.concerns: Long stretches of nihilism, cruelty between peers, sexual content with middle schoolers and a planned public suicide are well beyond what most families find age-appropriate.

frames_add.aligns: Judging the heart rather than the outward appearance (1 Samuel 16:7), breaking down the wall of hostility between two communities (Ephesians 2:14), honoring parents and answering insult without hatred (vol. 1-24).
frames_add.concerns: Teen dating is the center of the story, with a likely kiss (vol. 14) and a scene alone in Kaoruko's room (vol. 19) to check against family standards; no faith frame.

frames_add.aligns: Prejudice is undone by honest encounter, empathy and dialogue, with goodness that needs no religious grounding.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; some critics find the near-universal kindness idealized.

frames_add.aligns: Even the teacher who enforced the divide is given understandable reasons (vol. 24), modeling fairness to people who see things differently.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; religion appears only as seasonal custom (vol. 14).

frames_add.aligns: Loyal friends, a family bakery, respectful courtship that faces the parents (vol. 8) and everyday decency winning out over contempt.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond the teen-dating scenes in vol. 14 and vol. 19.

frames_add.aligns: Gentle care for an abandoned child (James 1:27), a guardian who will not kill even to save her (v8), and persecution of the 'unclean' condemned.
frames_add.concerns: A Christian-like church and a god called 'Heavenly Father' are framed as persecutors and schemers (v5, v9), and the gentle hero looks like a devil beside a dark 'Mother' in a lake.

frames_add.aligns: Kindness is shown with no promise of reward, and religious authority acting on revelation is exposed as fear turned into violence.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; gods and souls are real inside the fable, which does not lower the grade.

frames_add.aligns: The curse, the gods and Teacher's final choice are left as open mysteries, and the story wonders rather than preaches (v11).
frames_add.concerns: No sincere believer is shown admirably in the sources, so the church reads only as a persecutor.

frames_add.aligns: A guardian's love that outlasts memory and death, gentle everyday care, and forgiveness at the end.
frames_add.concerns: Steady dread, abandonment, and the loss of self in v8-9.

frames_add.aligns: Honesty after a deception, defending a friend who is mocked (vol. 3), an uncle who gives up his own dreams to raise his niece, and diligent work at music and exams are honored.
frames_add.concerns: The central romance between two girls is presented as the good life and continues into an unmarried couple living together (ch. 12), which most large Black denominations' teaching on marriage does not affirm, though families' views vary.

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is found through honest relationships, art and community, with no supernatural claims and no one punished for being who they are.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise beyond Mitsuki's early disguise (vol. 1), which the story defuses.

frames_add.aligns: A gentle story about dropping a false front and being accepted, with no preaching in any direction.
frames_add.concerns: Little to raise; the music industry's pressures are a mild talking point (ch. 12).

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty between friends, an uncle's sacrifice for family, and finding your own path through shared music reward everyday decency.
frames_add.concerns: A same-sex teen romance and adult cohabitation will be welcome to many families here and a question for some.

frames_add.aligns: Children bred as stock escape bondage and leave no one behind (ch. 32-37; Luke 15:4), mercy is offered to enemies, and a guilty mother repents and dies saving a child (ch. 176-177), close to the Exodus story of deliverance.
frames_add.concerns: A god-like being grants salvation as a bargain with a price rather than a gift (ch. 140-143), demons and their rites are central, and self-harm and suicide appear on the page (ch. 32-34, 173-174).

frames_add.aligns: The escape is won by reason, planning and testing assumptions, a thousand-year-old Promise kept for its own sake is broken and rewritten, and genocide is rejected.
frames_add.concerns: The final solution depends on a supernatural being's bargain, and the horror and suicide scenes need care for younger readers.

frames_add.aligns: Three leads argue three ethics fairly, sincere demon faith is honored while religion used for power is exposed, and the creator leaves interpretation to readers.
frames_add.concerns: Self-harm and suicide scenes (ch. 32-34, 173-174) call for a conversation.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to a chosen family, fairness even to enemies, hope and a reunion at the end (ch. 181) fit this tradition well.
frames_add.concerns: The horror premise and the self-harm and suicide scenes need an age check.

frames_add.aligns: A poor student studies and works his family out of debt, sisters stand by one another, apology restores a broken bond (ch. 86), and the romance ends in one faithful marriage (ch. 122).
frames_add.concerns: Fan service of high school girls in vol. 1, several kisses given without consent and played as romantic (ch. 102-108), and a drugged drink used as a prank (ch. 2, 44).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning comes from effort, learning and relationships, and each sister ends with a career she chose.
frames_add.concerns: Kisses without consent framed as romantic (ch. 102-108), early fan service of minors (vol. 1) and girls cast as interchangeable prizes.

frames_add.aligns: The author gives each sister closure rather than discarding the four not chosen, and readers are left to judge the choice.
frames_add.concerns: The harem framing goes unexamined, along with consent in the festival kisses and early fan service.

frames_add.aligns: Family loyalty ('the five of us'), honest work, apology and forgiveness, and a hopeful ending with a wedding.
frames_add.concerns: Early fan service and innuendo involving high school characters and kisses without asking are more than some families want for younger teens.

frames_add.aligns: A falsely accused man is raised up like Joseph (Genesis 39), prejudice against demi-humans is condemned, and the abused children of Raphtalia's village are protected and avenged (ch. 21-23).
frames_add.concerns: The hero buys a ten-year-old slave (ch. 2-3) and the story treats kindly owned slavery as practical, even turning the slave crest into a sign of devotion; public humiliation as justice (ch. 32) and coarse names.

frames_add.aligns: A self-deifying high priest and a racist church are exposed and defeated (ch. 28-30), and evidence and a fair hearing clear the hero.
frames_add.concerns: Slavery is treated as practical rather than wrong, and vengeance by public shaming is played as a payoff (ch. 32).

frames_add.aligns: The story targets a corrupt sect, not belief itself, and replaces it with a more inclusive church, leaving faith as such open.
frames_add.concerns: The hero's ownership of a child slave (ch. 2-3) is not examined, and the villains are drawn as wholly evil with no inner life.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to a found family, fairness restored, liars paid back, and a controlling church brought down (vol. 8).
frames_add.concerns: A child bought as a slave (ch. 2-3) and public humiliation played as satisfying payback (ch. 32).

frames_add.aligns: Loyal love, forgiveness of former enemies (Hendrickson, Dreyfus, Merlin) and deliverance of a kingdom from a cruel knighthood are rewarded, ending in faithful marriages (vol. 41).
frames_add.concerns: The hero is a demon prince, the setting's supreme deity is a tyrant, Christian moral names are inverted, and the hero's groping of the heroine (from ch. 1; ch. 79) is played as a joke.

frames_add.aligns: Chosen love and loyalty defeat both the gods and the demon king who forbid them, and prejudice between clans is overcome (vol. 27-41).
frames_add.concerns: Uninvited touching is a running gag without consequence (vol. 1-12), and battle remains the main solution.

frames_add.aligns: Neither heaven nor hell is shown as holding final truth, and characters on every side are given room to change.
frames_add.concerns: The harassment gag undercuts the respect the story preaches, and the dense mythology resolves by force.

frames_add.aligns: A found family of misfits, love that outlasts 107 lifetimes, and the dead returned to their loved ones reward loyalty and hope.
frames_add.concerns: The groping gag, frequent drinking at the tavern, and intense battles.

frames_add.aligns: A village's hidden sin and human sacrifice are exposed and condemned (vol. 5); repentance, apology and mercy to a lonely outsider (ch. 7, 16).
frames_add.concerns: A possessing spirit is befriended and folk deity worship is central; body-horror scenes between two high-school boys are written as sexual metaphor (vol. 1); same-sex feelings are treated sympathetically, which many families will want to discuss.

frames_add.aligns: Old rites are shown as useless or harmful, Tanaka and the library research test the legends, and a self is defined by relationships.
frames_add.concerns: Sexual metaphor involving teens and codependency raise consent and age questions; steady dread and a stabbing (ch. 16).

frames_add.aligns: Questions about the soul, identity and what a copy of a person is (the Swampman puzzle) are left honestly open.
frames_add.concerns: The same concerns about the teen scenes and about a bond that grows controlling.

frames_add.aligns: Loyalty to a friend and refusing to destroy the outsider; spirits and souls are taken seriously in a way many readers find meaningful.
frames_add.concerns: Constant dread, grief and codependency; folk worship shown as deadly; sexual metaphor with teens.

frames_add.aligns: A man leaves a life of crime and violence for a faithful, devoted marriage and honest work, a picture of a second chance (2 Corinthians 5:17), and former enemies are welcomed with hospitality.
frames_add.concerns: Profanity in the English editions and God's name misused once in the anime (Exodus 20:7); the criminal past is played for laughs rather than repented, and drug-deal gags recur.

frames_add.aligns: A person changes by his own choice and effort, violence is shown not to work, and the police who judge Tatsu by his looks are proved wrong.
frames_add.concerns: Organized crime is made lovable, which some families may want to discuss.

frames_add.aligns: Everyday decency, patience with people who misjudge him and care for others, with no preaching in any direction.
frames_add.concerns: Little; the gang past is treated lightly.

frames_add.aligns: Devotion to a spouse, loyalty to old friends without rejoining crime, neighborliness and pride in ordinary work.
frames_add.concerns: Coarse language and violence gags in the English editions.

frames_add.aligns: Worth is not earned by achievement, and Kusunoki turns from self-pity to carrying another's burden by paying Miyagi's debt (v3; Galatians 6:2).
frames_add.concerns: Selling one's life and the ending's chosen death are framed as fulfilment, with no hope beyond death and no turn to God or community in despair (v3).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is made in this life through chosen love and kindness, and the shop's price on a person is rejected in plain secular terms.
frames_add.concerns: A death-by-choice ending with no help-seeking shown needs mental-health framing for vulnerable readers (v3).

frames_add.aligns: The unexplained shop and the open question of whether the ending is fulfilment or surrender leave the reader room to decide.
frames_add.concerns: The suicide-adjacent premise (ch. 1) and ending (v3) may weigh on readers who feel hopeless.

frames_add.aligns: Everyday kindness and loyalty raise the worth of Kusunoki's life, a karma-like reversal that the shop itself records (v3).
frames_add.concerns: A long hopeless mood, Himeno's unresolved despair (v2) and both leads giving up their lives (v3) sit against the hope these families look for.

frames_add.aligns: Love that keeps going despite loss, a prince who walks to the gallows to save others (likely ch. 80-84), and hope that endures through suffering (Romans 5:3-5) are at the heart of the story.
frames_add.concerns: Reincarnation and talking with the dead are shown as real, the only major church persecutes and tortures (likely ch. 72-74), and Kahaku's self-destruction is framed as love and atonement (ch. 116).

frames_add.aligns: Meaning is made through human bonds, a finite life is valued over endless life, and a persecuting church and a cold creator are questioned rather than obeyed.
frames_add.concerns: Hayase's predatory obsession (likely ch. 45-54) and suicide-adjacent self-sacrifice (ch. 116) need careful framing.

frames_add.aligns: The creator is distant and ambiguous, rebirth and spirits are offered with wonder, and the biggest questions about suffering are left open.
frames_add.concerns: Frequent death and gore, and a self-destruction framed as noble.

frames_add.aligns: Loved ones who remain beyond death, reunions across lives, found family and a sense of fate reward hope and loyalty.
frames_add.concerns: Nearly every beloved character dies, including children, and Hayase's scenes are unsettling.

frames_add.aligns: Taking a life is grave and guilt is taken seriously (an echo of Cain and Abel), selfish wishes bring ruin, and Nene refuses to let another die in her place (ch. 71).
frames_add.concerns: The premise is summoning a ghost of the dead who grants wishes (ch. 1-3), with a chant children can copy and spirits as friends, which Holiness and Pentecostal families read against Deuteronomy 18:10-12; a forced kiss (ch. 105) and suicide-adjacent scenes (likely ch. 98-100).

frames_add.aligns: The value of finite life, responsibility for harm and refusing to trade one life for another are the story's moral core.
frames_add.concerns: Spirits and wish rituals are real within the story, and the summoning chant is a real school ritual some children may try.

frames_add.aligns: Teru's view that the dead must be kept apart and Kou's view that spirits can be helped both get reasons, and the afterlife is left mysterious.
frames_add.concerns: A forced kiss (ch. 105) and dark themes of fratricide and a short lifespan under a cute surface.

frames_add.aligns: Spirits, fate and the passage of the dead taken half-seriously, loyalty between friends, and a heroine who treasures the time she has.
frames_add.concerns: A boy who killed his twin, a forced kiss (ch. 105) and a friend's wish to die (likely ch. 98-100) need talking through.

frames_add.aligns: A hunted people is delivered from a purge run by a corrupt hidden elite (ch. 83, 127), enemies forgive one another, and the story ends with marriage, a child and a shared city (ch. 179).
